title: Animal life cycles: how young animals grow into adults

summary.text: A tadpole has a tail and gills, yet they grow into a frog with legs and lungs. Every animal's life goes through stages, from egg or baby to adult, and the adults make new young. This circle of stages is called a life cycle. A chick looks like a small hen and simply grows. But a tadpole and a caterpillar rebuild their whole bodies into a new shape. This big change is called metamorphosis, and it is switched on by chemical messages called hormones.
summary.art: Three circles side by side: an egg, a chick and a hen. Frogspawn, a tadpole, a froglet and a frog. An egg on a curry leaf, a caterpillar, a chrysalis and a butterfly, each circle with arrows going round.
summary.context: This card sums up the whole unit on animal life cycles in a few lines.

intro.hook: Here is a puzzle. A small animal lives in water. They breathe with gills, like a fish. They have a long tail and no legs. They scrape algae off stones. Algae are tiny water plants that make a green, slimy coat. A few weeks later, the very same animal breathes air, has four legs and no tail, and eats insects. Nobody swapped them. What happened?
intro.text: The animal is a tadpole, and they became a frog. In the monsoon, many ponds and puddles in India fill with tadpoles. In this unit you will open a hen's egg and find every part a chick needs. You will test whether air can pass through an eggshell. And you will find out where a tadpole's tail goes. It does not fall off.
intro.art: A monsoon puddle with black tadpoles wriggling in it, and on a stone at the edge, a tiny froglet with a stub of a tail.
intro.context: This is the way into the unit: a puzzle about an animal that changes their whole body.

outcomes: I can put the stages of a frog, a butterfly and a hen in order, and name each stage.
I can say what metamorphosis is: a big change where a young animal's body rebuilds into a new shape.
I can tell an animal that changes shape completely from one that just grows bigger, and give examples of each.
I can name the parts of a hen's egg and say what each part does for the growing chick.
I can watch an animal grow, measure them, record what I see in a table, and say what I think, what I saw and why.
I can explain that a new body is built from material already there: a chick from the yolk and white, a frog partly from their tail.
I can say what scientists agree about life cycles, and what they still do not know.
I can say that hormones are chemical messages that switch the change on, and that a caterpillar and the butterfly they become have the same genes.

terms.meaning: All the stages of an animal's life, in order. The last stage makes eggs or babies, so the cycle starts again.

terms.meaning: The young stage of an insect that looks very different from the adult. Two or more are called larvae.
terms.example: A caterpillar is the larva of a butterfly. A wriggler is the larva of a mosquito.

terms.meaning: The resting stage of an insect, between larva and adult. Inside, the body is rebuilt. Two or more are called pupae.

explanations.definition: A life cycle is all the stages an animal goes through in their life, in order. The adults make eggs or babies, so the cycle goes round again.
explanations.description: Every animal started small. A hen started as an egg. You started as a single cell, smaller than a full stop. Each animal goes through stages, one after another. The last stage is the adult. Adults make eggs or babies, and those young grow up and make young of their own. That is why we draw a life cycle as a circle, not a line.
examples: A hen lays an egg. A chick hatches. The chick grows into a hen. The hen lays eggs.
A cow has a calf. The calf grows into a cow. The cow has a calf.
A frog lays frogspawn in a pond. Tadpoles hatch, become frogs, and lay frogspawn.
explanations.art: A big circle of arrows with a hen, an egg and a chick on it, and a smaller circle with a cow and a calf.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what a life cycle is.

explanations.concept: The hen: an egg, a chick and a hen
explanations.definition: A hen's life cycle has three stages: egg, chick and adult. The chick looks like a small, fluffy hen. They grow bigger without changing their shape.
explanations.description: A hen lays an egg. If a rooster has mated with her, the egg can grow a chick. The hen sits on her eggs to keep them warm, about as warm as your body. She turns them with her beak many times a day. Inside, the chick grows for 21 days. They use the yolk as food and the egg white for water and more food. On day 21 the chick pecks a crack with a tiny hard tip on their beak, called the egg tooth. They push their way out, wet and tired. In a few hours they are dry and fluffy, and they can walk and peck. At about five or six months old, a young hen lays her first egg.
examples: Most shop eggs come from farms with no roosters. These eggs are not fertilised, so they can never hatch.
A chick follows the first moving thing they see, usually their mother. They learn to peck by copying her.
Wild chickens still live in Indian forests. They are called red junglefowl. Farm chickens come mainly from them.
explanations.art: Three pictures: a hen sitting on eggs, a wet chick breaking out of a shell, and a fluffy chick pecking near their mother.
explanations.context: This card is about the life cycle of a hen, which has no big change of shape.

explanations.definition: An egg is a complete home and food store for a growing chick. Each part has a job.
explanations.description: A chick growing in an egg has three problems. They need food for three weeks, they need air, and they must not be squashed. Each part of the egg solves one of these. The yellow ball is the yolk. It is the chick's food. On top of the yolk is a tiny white spot. In a fertilised egg, this is where the chick begins. The clear egg white holds water and cushions the yolk. Two twisted white cords, called chalazae, hold the yolk in the middle. Under the shell are two thin skins, called membranes. At the round end they come apart and leave a pocket of air. The shell looks solid, but it has thousands of tiny holes, so air can pass in and out.
examples: The air pocket is at the fat, round end of the egg. The chick's beak pokes into it just before hatching.
Put a raw egg in very hot water, and tiny bubbles come out of the shell. The warmed air inside is escaping through the holes.
Brown and white eggs are the same inside. The shell colour depends on the kind of hen.
A growing chick takes calcium from the inside of their shell to build their bones. The shell gets thinner, which makes hatching easier.
explanations.art: A cut-open egg with labels: shell with tiny holes, two skins, air pocket at the round end, white, twisted cords, yolk and a tiny white spot.
explanations.context: This card explains what each part of a hen's egg does for the chick growing inside.

explanations.concept: The frog: from tadpole to frog
explanations.definition: A frog's life cycle has four main stages: frogspawn, tadpole, froglet and adult frog. The tadpole changes their whole body to become a frog. This is metamorphosis.
explanations.description: In the monsoon, a female frog lays hundreds or thousands of eggs in water. Each egg sits in a ball of jelly. A male frog fertilises them. After a few days, tiny tadpoles wriggle out. At first they breathe with feathery gills, and they eat green slime and soft plants. Then the change begins. Back legs grow first. Then the front legs pop out. Lungs grow inside, so the young frog can breathe air. Their mouth gets wider and their gut gets shorter, ready to eat insects. Their tail gets shorter every day. Now they are a froglet. Soon the tail is gone, and the frog hops onto land. In many Indian frogs, all this takes one to three months.
examples: Indian bullfrogs and common toads breed in rain puddles and ponds after the first monsoon showers.
A tadpole has gills like a fish. A frog has lungs, and can also breathe through their wet skin.
Some frogs in the Western Ghats skip the tadpole stage. Tiny froglets hatch straight out of their eggs on land.
explanations.art: A circle: floating frogspawn, a tadpole with gills, a tadpole with back legs, a froglet with four legs and a tail stub, an adult frog.
explanations.context: This card is about the life cycle of a frog, and how a tadpole changes into a frog.

explanations.concept: The butterfly: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and butterfly
explanations.definition: A butterfly has four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult. The larva is called a caterpillar. The pupa is called a chrysalis. This is complete metamorphosis.
explanations.description: A lime butterfly lays a tiny round egg on a curry leaf or a lemon leaf. Her caterpillars can eat only leaves of this plant family, and she will never feed them. So she lays each egg right on the caterpillar's food. After a few days, a caterpillar chews their way out. Often they eat their own eggshell first. Then they eat leaves all day. Their skin cannot stretch much, so they grow a new skin underneath and wriggle out of the old one. This is called moulting. They moult four times. After two or three weeks, they stop eating. They tie themself to a stem with a silk belt and moults one last time. Under that skin is the chrysalis. For about ten days they hang still while their body is rebuilt inside. Then the chrysalis splits, and a butterfly climbs out. They pump blood into their crumpled wings, wait for them to dry, and flies.
examples: Birds eat caterpillars. Young lime caterpillars are brown and white, like bird droppings, so birds leave them alone.
Older lime caterpillars are green, the colour of the leaves they eat.
A grown butterfly does not grow any more. They drink nectar, find a mate and lay eggs.
explanations.art: A circle: a tiny egg on a curry leaf, a brown-and-white caterpillar, a green caterpillar, a green chrysalis on a stem, a black-and-yellow lime butterfly.
explanations.context: This card is about the life cycle of a butterfly, which has four very different stages.

explanations.concept: Metamorphosis: a body that rebuilds itself
explanations.definition: Metamorphosis is a big change of body shape after hatching. The young animal's body takes parts of itself apart and builds new parts, often from the same material.
explanations.description: When a tadpole's tail gets shorter, it does not drop off. The cells of the tail break themselves down. Other cells swallow the pieces, and the blood carries the material to the growing legs, lungs and head. During the biggest changes the tadpole stops eating, and lives on their own tail. Inside a chrysalis, most of the caterpillar's body is broken down too. But small groups of cells have been waiting inside the caterpillar since they hatched. One group becomes a wing, another a leg, another an eye. They grow fast, using the broken-down caterpillar as their building material. So the butterfly is built out of the caterpillar.
examples: A tadpole's tail is taken back into their body and used again.
The wings of a butterfly start as tiny flat pockets of cells inside the caterpillar.
Your body rebuilds itself too, slowly. The skin cells on top are rubbed off all the time and replaced from underneath.
explanations.art: A tadpole with their tail fading into tiny dots that flow along arrows into their growing legs. Next to the tadpole, a caterpillar outline with small glowing patches where wings and legs will grow.
explanations.context: This card explains metamorphosis, the big change that turns a tadpole into a frog and a caterpillar into a butterfly.

explanations.definition: Some animals just grow bigger. Some change a little, step by step. Some change completely, with a resting pupa stage in the middle.
explanations.description: Scientists sort life cycles into three kinds. In the first kind, the baby looks like a small adult and just grows. Hens, cows, snakes and people grow up like this. In the second kind there are three stages: egg, nymph and adult. A nymph looks like a small adult without wings. Each time they moult, their wings grow a bit more. In the third kind there are four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult. The larva looks nothing like the adult. Frogs have no pupa, but their tadpoles change completely, so frogs go through metamorphosis too.
examples: Just grows: hen, cow, snake, crocodile, human.
Egg, nymph, adult: grasshopper, cockroach, dragonfly.
Egg, larva, pupa, adult: butterfly, silkworm moth, mosquito, ladybird, honeybee.
explanations.art: Three rows: a chick growing into a hen. A small wingless grasshopper growing into a winged one. A caterpillar, chrysalis and butterfly.
explanations.context: This card sorts animals into three kinds, by how they grow up.

explanations.description: Why would an animal rebuild their whole body? Scientists have three main ideas. First, each stage can be good at one job. A caterpillar is built for eating. A butterfly is built for flying to find mates and new plants. Second, the young and the adults do not compete for food. Tadpoles eat slime in water, and frogs eat insects on land. Third, it helps the young spread out. Caterpillars cannot travel far, but butterflies can fly to new places. These ideas fit what we see. But nobody can go back in time to watch how metamorphosis began.
examples: A caterpillar eats leaves. A butterfly drinks nectar. They never fight over food.
Tadpoles live in water and frogs on land, so they use two different homes.
Mosquito wrigglers eat tiny specks of food in water, such as microbes. Adult mosquitoes fly and drink plant juices, and females also drink blood to make eggs.
explanations.art: Split picture: below a pond line, tadpoles nibbling slime on a stone. Above it, a frog catching a fly with their tongue.
explanations.context: This card asks why some animals change their whole body as they grow up. Scientists have ideas but no final answer.

explanations.definition: A hormone is a chemical message carried in the blood. Hormones tell a young animal's body when to start changing.
explanations.description: How does a tadpole know when to become a frog? A small part of their neck, called the thyroid, makes a hormone. When there is enough of this hormone in the blood, the change starts. Legs grow, the gills go and the tail shrinks. In 1912, a scientist named Friedrich Gudernatsch fed tadpoles a little dried thyroid from a horse. They turned into tiny frogs much too early. Insects use different hormones, but they work the same way. A caterpillar and the butterfly they become have exactly the same genes. Genes are the instructions inside every cell. Hormones switch on different instructions at different times, so one set of genes builds two very different bodies.
examples: Your thyroid makes the same hormone as a tadpole's. It helps you grow. It needs iodine, which is why salt in India has iodine added.
Tadpoles in warm water usually change sooner than tadpoles in cold water.
If you test the genes of a caterpillar and of the butterfly they became, they match exactly.
explanations.art: A tadpole with a small glowing spot in their neck, sending glowing dots through their body towards new legs.
explanations.context: This card explains how a young animal's body knows when to change: chemical messages called hormones.

explanations.concept: Are they still the same animal?
explanations.description: A caterpillar is broken down and rebuilt into a butterfly. So is the butterfly the same animal as the caterpillar? People have argued about questions like this for thousands of years. Scientists have found one clue: some memories may survive the change.
examples: The butterfly has the same genes as the caterpillar.
Much of the caterpillar's body is broken down, but parts of their nerves are kept and rebuilt.
Most of your body is made of different material from when you were a baby. Are you still the same person?

perspectives.explanation: Yes, they are the same animal. They are one living thing all the way through, with one set of genes. They just have two very different bodies at two times of their life.

perspectives.who: Douglas Blackiston, Elena Silva Casey and Martha Weiss, scientists in the USA, in 2008
perspectives.explanation: They taught caterpillars of a moth to stay away from one smell. After metamorphosis, many of the adult moths still stayed away from it. So some memory may pass through the chrysalis. Other scientists want more tests before they are sure.

Some philosophers say an animal stays the same one because their life goes on without a break, even while their material and their shape change. Others say there is no simple answer, and it depends on what you mean by 'the same'.

explanations.art: A caterpillar and a butterfly facing each other, with a dotted thought bubble joining them.
explanations.context: This card asks a deep question: when a caterpillar becomes a butterfly, are they still the same animal?

explanations.concept: Maria Sibylla Merian: watching, not guessing
explanations.definition: People once believed that caterpillars and flies grew out of mud, dew or rotting food. Careful watching showed that every insect hatches from an egg laid by a parent.
explanations.description: Maria Sibylla Merian was born in Germany in 1647. At 13, she began raising caterpillars at home. She painted each one with their eggs, their chrysalis and the plant they ate. In 1679 she published a book on how caterpillars change into butterflies and moths. At 52, she sailed to Suriname in South America with her daughter to study insects there. For a long time people called her an artist, not a scientist. Today she is honoured as one of the first people to study life cycles properly.
examples: Merian painted the plant each caterpillar ate, because she saw that the mother butterfly chooses that plant.
A Dutch scientist, Jan Swammerdam, cut open caterpillars in the 1660s. He found folded wings already growing inside.
explanations.art: Maria Sibylla Merian at a wooden table with a magnifying glass, a caterpillar on a leaf and her painting of the same caterpillar beside it.
explanations.context: This card tells the true story of Maria Sibylla Merian, who studied how caterpillars change.

explanations.concept: Going further out: the material goes round
explanations.description: A life cycle is a circle of animals. The material in them goes round in a bigger circle. A caterpillar eats leaves, and the leaves were built from air, water and sunlight. When a butterfly dies, small animals and microbes break their body down. Their atoms go back into the soil and air, and plants take them up again. So the atoms in a butterfly's wing may once have been in a frog, a hen or a person. Almost all the atoms in an egg, apart from hydrogen, were made inside stars long ago.
examples: Leaves that fall become soil. The soil feeds new plants.
The calcium in an eggshell came from the hen's food, and before that from rocks.
Scientists agree that the carbon and oxygen in your body were made in stars.
explanations.art: A big loop: a star exploding, dust becoming a planet, a plant, a caterpillar, a butterfly, a fallen butterfly in soil, and back to a plant.
explanations.context: This card follows life cycles out to the soil, the Earth and the stars.

explanations.description: Scientists are not sure how complete metamorphosis first began, more than 300 million years ago. They do not know exactly how each waiting cell inside a caterpillar knows which part to become. They are not sure how much a butterfly remembers of being a caterpillar. And nobody knows what being a chrysalis feels like from the inside.
examples: Fossils show that insects with larvae lived more than 300 million years ago.
Scientists are still testing which memories survive in moths and beetles.
Some frogs skip the tadpole stage, and scientists study why.
explanations.art: A chrysalis hanging from a twig with a big question mark drawn faintly inside it.
explanations.context: This card lists questions about life cycles that scientists still cannot answer.

agreed.text: Every animal comes from a parent or parents, usually starting as an egg. Animals do not grow out of mud or rotting food.
agreed.evidence: Francesco Redi showed in 1668 that maggots grow only where flies can lay eggs. Since then, scientists have watched the life cycles of thousands of kinds of animals.
agreed.context: This card is about something scientists agree on about animal life cycles, and how they know.

agreed.text: Frogs, butterflies and many other animals go through metamorphosis. Their young look very different from the adults.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can watch it. People raise tadpoles and caterpillars at home and in classrooms every year, and see the same stages.
agreed.context: This card is about something scientists agree on about animal life cycles, and how they know.

agreed.text: Metamorphosis is switched on by hormones, chemical messages in the blood.
agreed.evidence: In 1912, tadpoles fed thyroid changed into frogs early. In 1916, tadpoles whose thyroid had been removed stayed tadpoles.
agreed.context: This card is about something scientists agree on about animal life cycles, and how they know.

agreed.text: A tadpole's tail and much of a caterpillar's body are broken down and reused to build the new body.
agreed.evidence: Scientists can watch the tail cells break apart under a microscope. Tadpoles stop eating while their tails shrink.
agreed.context: This card is about something scientists agree on about animal life cycles, and how they know.

agreed.text: A caterpillar and the butterfly they become are one living thing with exactly the same genes.
agreed.evidence: Gene tests on the larva and the adult give the same result. Only which genes are switched on is different.
agreed.context: This card is about something scientists agree on about animal life cycles, and how they know.

agreed.text: A chick takes about 21 days to grow inside their egg, if the egg is kept warm and turned.
agreed.evidence: Poultry farmers have hatched millions of chicks in warm boxes called incubators. The timing is the same almost every time.
agreed.context: This card is about something scientists agree on about animal life cycles, and how they know.

challenging.claim: Small animals, like flies and caterpillars, grow out of mud, dew or rotting food.
challenging.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker who lived about 2,350 years ago, and most people for about 2,000 years after him.
challenging.for: It looks true. Leave food out, and maggots appear. Nobody sees the tiny eggs being laid.
challenging.against: Francesco Redi covered meat jars with thin cloth in 1668. No maggots grew in them. Maria Sibylla Merian and others watched insects lay eggs and raised the young. Every animal comes from an egg or a parent.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of where small animals come from, and why scientists gave it up.

challenging.claim: Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar turns completely into soup.
challenging.who: Many books, websites and teachers say this.
challenging.for: If you open a chrysalis a few days in, much of the inside is runny. Most of the caterpillar's body really is broken down.
challenging.against: Not everything becomes soup. The small groups of waiting cells stay whole and grow into wings, legs and eyes. Parts of the nerves and breathing tubes are kept and rebuilt.
challenging.context: This card looks at a popular idea about what happens inside a chrysalis.

challenging.claim: A butterfly comes out of a cocoon.
challenging.who: A very common mistake, even in some famous picture books.
challenging.for: Moths do come out of cocoons. Both are cases that hold a pupa, so people mix them up.
challenging.against: A cocoon is a silk case that a moth caterpillar spins around themself. Most butterfly caterpillars spin no silk case. Their own hard skin is the chrysalis.
challenging.context: This card is about the difference between a cocoon and a chrysalis.

challenging.claim: Caterpillars began when an ancient insect mated with a worm-like animal, and their two life cycles joined.
challenging.who: Donald Williamson, a British scientist, from the 1990s to the 2000s.
challenging.for: It would explain why a larva and an adult look like two different animals.
challenging.against: Gene studies show that a caterpillar's genes come from their insect parents, like all their other genes. No sign of another animal's genes has been found. Most scientists reject the idea.
challenging.context: This card is about an unusual idea of how caterpillars first began.

challenging.claim: A caterpillar is like a baby that hatched very early, before they had finished growing in the egg.
challenging.who: James Truman and Lynn Riddiford, two scientists in the USA, in 1999.
challenging.for: The waiting cells in a caterpillar are like the parts of an embryo that have not grown yet. The same hormones are involved in both.
challenging.against: It is hard to test something that began more than 300 million years ago. Other scientists have different ideas about how the pupa stage began.
challenging.context: This card is about one scientific idea of how complete metamorphosis first began.

challenging.claim: If you touch a tadpole or a caterpillar, they will die.
challenging.for: It is true that soft young animals are easily hurt. Tadpoles need wet skin, and squeezing a caterpillar can harm them.
challenging.against: A gentle touch with a wet hand does not usually kill them. But it does stress them, so look and don't handle. Soap, sunscreen or salt on your hands can harm a tadpole's skin.
challenging.context: This card looks at a common worry about touching young animals.

story.title: Where the Tails Go
story.note: Everything about the tadpoles is real: back legs first, the tadpole stopping eating, and the tail being broken down and used again. Kavya, Farida, their town near the Western Ghats and their bucket are made up.
text: The first monsoon rain came to Kavya's town in the middle of the night. It came so hard that it woke her up. By morning the empty plot behind the water tank had turned into a brown, shining pond. By the next evening it was singing.
"Frogs," said Farida, from the wall. Farida lived in the next building. She had been Kavya's best friend for four years, which was half of their whole lives. "Hundreds of them. Listen."
They listened. The singing sounded like a hundred people trying to start a hundred scooters.

Three days later there were clumps of clear jelly floating at the edge of the pond, each little ball with a black dot inside. Three days after that, the dots had become commas. Then the commas began to wriggle.
"We should keep some," said Kavya. "Just a few. Just to see."

Kavya's mother said yes, on two conditions. They had to use pond water, never tap water. And they had to put every single one back in the pond when it was done. So the girls filled an old blue bucket with pond water and a stone with green slime on it. They scooped up five tadpoles in a steel tumbler. They named them after the five fingers of a hand. Thumb, Pointer, Tall, Ring and Little.

Farida had a notebook. She drew lines in it and made a table, because that is the kind of person Farida was. Every second day they measured each tadpole, as gently as they could, against a ruler held outside the bucket. Body. Tail. Legs, none.
It was on the ninth day, while they were measuring, that Farida said it. "We're moving. In September. Abbu got a job in Hyderabad."
Kavya held the ruler very still.
"It's only September," said Farida. "That's ages."
It was not ages. It was eleven weeks. Kavya counted.

After that, Kavya did not want to look at the table. But Farida kept filling it in, every second day, in her neat small numbers. Body, 9 millimetres. Tail, 16. Then, on day fifteen, beside Tall's name, she drew two tiny lines. Back legs.

By day twenty-two all five had back legs. They looked like tadpoles who had put on shorts. Then one morning, Pointer's front legs popped out, both at once, like a child pulling arms out through a jumper.
And then the tails began to go.
Kavya noticed it first. She was not looking at the notebook. She was looking at the bucket. "Thumb's tail is shorter," she said. "Look. It's broken."
Farida looked at the numbers. Thumb's tail had been 18 millimetres. Now it was 14.

"Something is biting them," said Kavya. "Or the tails are falling off." She tipped the bucket a little towards the light and looked at the bottom. There was the slimy stone. There was some mud. There were no tails.
"Maybe the others ate it," said Farida.

That was a horrible thought. They watched for a long time. Nobody bit anybody. The tadpoles just hung in the water, very still, their new legs dangling. And there was something else. The girls dropped in a pinch of boiled spinach, the way they always did. The tadpoles did not eat it. Not one of them.
"They're sick," said Kavya. Her voice went small. "They're not eating and their tails are breaking and they're going to die."
But Farida had turned back three pages in the notebook. She ran her finger down the numbers, and then down them again.
"Kavya," she said. "Look at Little."

Little had been the smallest. His tail had gone from 15 millimetres, to 12, to 8. But it had not gone in one snap, the way a broken thing would go. It had gone a little at a time, every single day. And all that time his front legs had been getting longer and fatter. His head had been getting wider. His mouth, which had been a tiny round sucker, was turning into a wide frog's grin.
"It's not falling off," said Farida slowly. "It's going in."
Kavya looked at Little. She looked at the empty bottom of the bucket. She thought about the spinach, uneaten.
"They don't need to eat," she said. "They've got lunch."
"Their own tails," said Farida.
"They're eating their own tails from the inside," said Kavya. "And making legs out of them."
It was the most disgusting and the most wonderful thing either of them had ever heard. They laughed until Kavya's mother came to see what was wrong.

Later, Kavya's mother found a page on her phone and read it to them. She said it was true. The tail cells break themselves down, and the blood carries the material away to the growing frog. Nothing is thrown out. The tadpole doesn't lose their tail. They turn it into the frog.

Seven days later, Little was sitting on the slimy stone with his head out of the water. He had a stub of tail no bigger than a grain of rice. He was looking at the sky, which he had never seen before, with eyes that had been built for air.

They carried the five froglets back to the pond in the steel tumbler, all together, on a Sunday at the end of August. The pond was smaller now and full of grass. The froglets climbed out onto the mud, one by one, and sat there blinking. Then Thumb hopped, and then they all did, into the grass, and were gone.
Farida closed the notebook. It was full.
"You keep it," she said.
"It's yours. You made the table."
"You noticed the tails," said Farida. "Anyway, I'll make a new one in Hyderabad. They have frogs there too. Probably."

In September, Farida moved. Kavya did not cry at the gate, though she did cry later, a bit. That night she lay in bed and listened to the frogs behind the water tank. There were not hundreds now. There were a few. Somewhere in the grass, five small frogs were not singing yet. They would be, in a year or two, with lungs and wide mouths built partly out of tails.
She thought that she should write to Farida about it. She thought that when she did, she would not write that something was lost. She would write that something had gone in.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the tadpoles look as if they are breaking, but they are rebuilding. The tail's cells break down, and the body reuses the material to build a frog. That is why the tadpoles stop eating. The girls work this out from their records, not by a lucky guess: the numbers show the tail shrinking a little each day, not snapping. The story also asks whether a friendship can change shape without being lost.
ask: Why did Kavya think the tadpoles were sick? What did Farida's notebook show instead?
Why did the tadpoles stop eating spinach when their tails were shrinking?
Where did the tadpoles' tails go?
Why did Kavya's mother say to use pond water and to put every tadpole back?
At the end, Kavya decides to write that something 'had gone in', not that something was lost. What do you think she means?

printables.title: A playing mat with five circles, one per animal

rules: Cut out the 20 stage cards. Shuffle them. Deal 4 cards to each player. Put the rest face down in a pile.
Your aim is to collect all 4 stages of one animal and lay them on that animal's circle in the right order.

On your turn, do one of two things. Take the top card from the pile and then put one card you don't need face up on a discard pile. Or ask another player for a stage you need, for example: 'Do you have Butterfly 3, the chrysalis?'
If they have the card you asked for, they give it to you, and you give them one card you don't need. So everyone always holds 4 cards.
When you have all 4 stages of an animal, lay them on the animal's circle in order and tell that animal's life story. Then take a question card and answer it. Then take 4 new cards from the pile.
If the pile runs out, shuffle the discard pile and use it as the new pile.
The game ends when all five animals are laid down. The player who laid down the most animals wins.

flow.say: These cards show five animals at different ages. Before we play, let's look. Which pictures look nothing like the grown-up animal?
flow.kid: Look at all the cards. Find the ones that look nothing like the grown-up animal. How many can you find?

ask.q: Which young animals look nothing like their parents?
good: The tadpole.
The caterpillar.
The mosquito wriggler.
The chrysalis.

flow.context: This is the first step of Who Comes Next?, a card game about life cycles. First you look at all the cards together.

flow.do: Take out the four hen cards. Ask your child to put them in order, as a practice round.

check.q: In a hen's life cycle, what comes straight after the egg?
check.why: A chick hatches straight out of the egg. They already look like a small, fluffy hen, so a hen has no larva and no tadpole. Picking 'larva' usually means thinking every animal changes shape. Only some do, like butterflies and mosquitoes.

flow.do: 1. Shuffle all 20 stage cards. Deal 4 to each player. 2. Take turns by the rules. 3. When someone completes an animal, they tell that animal's story and answer a question card.
flow.say: When you complete an animal, tell us their life story, like this. 'First, a tiny egg on a curry leaf. Then a caterpillar hatches and eats.'
flow.kid: Play! Collect all four stages of one animal. Lay them in order. Then tell their life story out loud.
flow.parent: Listen for the stage names. Good stories include a change: 'the tadpole grows legs and their tail goes in'. If your child puts the chrysalis before the caterpillar, ask: 'Who makes the chrysalis?' The caterpillar does, so they must come first.

flow.do: When the mosquito or grasshopper is completed, stop and compare that animal with the butterfly.
flow.say: The mosquito has four stages, like the butterfly. The grasshopper has only three different shapes. Their babies look like small grasshoppers without wings.
flow.kid: Compare the grasshopper and the butterfly. Which one has a resting stage that doesn't eat?

check.q: Which animal has a pupa, a resting stage, in their life cycle?
check.why: A mosquito has four stages: egg, wriggler, tumbler and adult. The tumbler is their pupa. A grasshopper has no pupa. Their young are nymphs that grow wings slowly. Picking 'grasshopper' usually means thinking all insects grow up the same way.

flow.do: Count each player's completed animals. Then ask the closing question.
flow.say: Who won? Now, everyone, tell me. Which animal's life would you most like to live, and why?
flow.kid: Who laid down the most animals? They win! Which animal's life would you like to live? Why?
flow.think: If you were a caterpillar, would you want to become a butterfly? Would you still be you?

check.q: Frog square 10 says 'Stop eating: your tail feeds you.' What does that mean?

worksheets.title: Life Cycle Detective (core)

items.p: What is a life cycle?
opts: All the stages of an animal's life, in order, going round again
items.why: A life cycle is all the stages, from egg or baby to adult, and the adult makes new eggs or babies. Picking 'how long an animal lives' mixes up a life cycle with a lifespan. A lifespan is just a number of years.

items.p: Put the stages of a butterfly in order, starting at the beginning: butterfly, caterpillar, egg, chrysalis.
items.why: A butterfly lays an egg. A caterpillar hatches and eats. They make a chrysalis. A butterfly comes out. Then they lay eggs, and the cycle starts again.
items.art: Four small pictures in a row: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly.

items.p: Put the stages of a frog in order: froglet, frogspawn, adult frog, tadpole.
items.why: Frogspawn hatches into tadpoles. Tadpoles grow legs and become froglets. Froglets lose their tails and become frogs.

items.p: Put the stages of a hen in order: chick, hen, egg.
items.why: A chick hatches from an egg and grows into a hen. A hen has only three stages, because the chick does not change shape.

items.p: A young frog that lives in water and swims with a tail is called a ____.
items.why: A tadpole is the young of a frog or toad. They live in water and breathe with gills at first.

items.p: The big change in body shape, like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly, is called ____.
items.why: Metamorphosis means a big change of shape. The young animal's body rebuilds itself into a new form.

items.p: The yellow part of an egg, which is food for the chick, is called the ____.
items.why: The yolk is the chick's food store. The growing chick uses it up over 21 days.

items.p: Sort these animals. Do their babies look like small adults, or do they change shape completely?
items.why: Chicks, calves and puppies look like small versions of their parents. Tadpoles, caterpillars and mosquito wrigglers look nothing like their parents, and go through metamorphosis.

items.p: Match each baby to their grown-up.
items.why: Each young animal grows into their own kind of adult. Some look very different, like the wriggler and the mosquito.

items.p: A butterfly comes out of a cocoon.
items.why: False. A butterfly comes out of a chrysalis, which is the pupa's own hard skin. A cocoon is a silk case that a moth caterpillar spins around themself.

items.p: A tadpole's tail falls off when they become a frog.
items.why: False. The tail gets shorter a little each day. Its cells are broken down and the body uses the material to build the frog. Nothing drops off.

items.p: Eggs from a farm with no rooster will hatch if you keep them warm.
items.why: False. With no rooster, the eggs are not fertilised. They can never grow a chick, however warm they are kept. Most shop eggs come from farms like this.

items.p: In the eggshell bubbles experiment, bubbles came out of an egg in very hot water. What does this tell us?
opts: The shell has tiny holes that let air through
The shell is made of air
items.why: The hot water warmed the air inside the egg. Warm air takes up more space, so it pushed out through thousands of tiny holes in the shell. A growing chick breathes through the same holes. Picking 'the egg was cooking' is a natural guess, because bubbles often mean boiling. But the water was not boiling, and the bubbles came from the shell.
items.context: In the eggshell bubbles experiment, you put one egg in very hot water and one in cold water, and looked for bubbles.

items.p: Which stage of a butterfly does most of the eating?
items.why: The caterpillar eats leaves all day and grows fast. The chrysalis does not eat at all. The butterfly only sips nectar. Picking 'the butterfly' is a common guess, because that is the stage we see most.

items.p: Draw the life cycle of a frog as a circle. Draw and label four stages, with arrows between them.
items.a: Frogspawn, then a tadpole, then a froglet with legs and a short tail, then an adult frog, with an arrow back to frogspawn.
items.why: A life cycle is drawn as a circle, because the adult frog lays frogspawn and the cycle starts again.
items.art: An empty circle with four boxes on it and arrows between them.

items.p: Your friend says, 'A caterpillar and a butterfly are two different animals.' What would you tell them?
items.a: They are the same animal at two different stages of their life. The caterpillar makes a chrysalis, and their body is rebuilt into the butterfly. They even have the same genes.
items.why: Metamorphosis changes the body, but it is one animal all the way through. Scientists check this with genes, which match exactly.

worksheets.context: This worksheet checks the main ideas of the unit: the stages of a frog, a butterfly and a hen, and what metamorphosis is.

worksheets.title: Inside the Change (stretch)

items.p: A grasshopper's babies look like small grasshoppers without wings. Which kind of life cycle is this?
opts: Egg, nymph, adult, with no pupa
items.why: A young grasshopper is a nymph. They look like a small adult, and their wings grow a bit more each time they moult. They have no pupa. Picking 'just grows' is close. But a grasshopper sheds their whole skin to grow, and their wings appear bit by bit. A chick hatches with their wings already there.

items.p: Why does a caterpillar moult?
opts: Their skin is too tight because they have grown
They are turning into a frog
items.why: A caterpillar's skin can't stretch much. They grow a new, bigger skin underneath, and wriggle out of the old one. Picking 'a new colour' is a fair guess, because a lime caterpillar does change colour after a moult. But the reason they moult is to grow.

items.p: Which part of a hen's egg gives the chick their first breath of air before hatching?
opts: The air pocket at the round end
items.why: Two skins under the shell come apart at the round end, making an air pocket. Just before hatching, the chick pokes their beak in and starts breathing with their lungs. Picking 'the white' is a natural guess, because the white is clear. But the white is mostly water, not air.
items.context: In Open an Egg like a Scientist, you cracked an egg and found all its parts.

items.p: In Tadpole Watch, the tadpoles stopped eating while their tails got shorter. Why?
opts: They were living on the material from their own tails
They didn't like the spinach any more
items.why: The tail is broken down and its material is used to build the frog. Meanwhile, the mouth and gut are being rebuilt for eating insects. Picking 'sick' is a natural worry. But sick tadpoles don't grow new legs and lungs.
items.context: Tadpole Watch is a six-week monsoon experiment. You keep a few tadpoles in pond water and measure them every second day.

items.p: Look at this chart of one tadpole's tail length. What happened to the tail?
opts: It grew, then shrank a little at a time
It fell off in one go on day 30
items.why: The line goes up to 18 millimetres by day 20, then comes down step by step: 14, 8, then 2. A tail that fell off would drop to zero in one step. Picking 'fell off in one go' is what most people expect, before they measure.
items.context: In Tadpole Watch, children measured a tadpole's tail every few days. These numbers are made up, to show the pattern.

chart.title: Made-up example: one tadpole's tail length

items.p: A chick takes about ____ days to grow inside their egg.
items.why: About 21 days, which is three weeks, if the egg is kept warm and turned.

items.p: A chemical message carried in the blood, which tells a tadpole when to change, is called a ____.
items.why: A hormone is a chemical message. A tadpole's thyroid makes the hormone that starts their metamorphosis.

items.p: Match each part of an egg to its job.
pairs: hold the yolk in the middle
protects, and lets air in through tiny holes
items.why: Every part of an egg does a job for the growing chick. Together they make a complete home and food store.
items.context: In Open an Egg like a Scientist, you cracked an egg and found all its parts.

items.p: Sort these insects by their life cycle.
items.why: Butterflies, mosquitoes and bees have a pupa stage. Grasshoppers, cockroaches and dragonflies do not. Their nymphs grow wings slowly.

items.p: A caterpillar and the butterfly they become have exactly the same genes.
items.why: True. Genes are the instructions in every cell. They are the same all through their life. Hormones switch different instructions on at different times.

items.p: Inside a chrysalis, absolutely everything turns into soup.
items.why: False. Much of the caterpillar's body is broken down. But the waiting cells stay whole and grow into wings, legs and eyes, and some parts are kept and rebuilt.

items.p: In the Naked Egg experiment, the egg stayed whole after the shell was gone.
items.why: True. Two thin, strong skins under the shell held it together.
items.context: In the Naked Egg experiment, you left an egg in vinegar for two days until its shell was gone.

items.p: Why does a lime butterfly lay her eggs on a curry leaf or lemon plant, and not on any plant?
items.a: Her caterpillars can only eat leaves from that plant family. She never meets her babies, so she lays them right on their food.
items.why: Choosing the plant is the only care a butterfly mother gives. Maria Sibylla Merian noticed this in the 1600s and painted each caterpillar with their plant.
items.context: In the Curry Leaf Hunt, you looked for lime butterfly eggs and caterpillars on curry leaf and lemon plants.

items.p: In the dough model, you squashed a caterpillar into a ball and built a butterfly from it. What does the model show? What does it get wrong?
items.a: It shows that the butterfly is built from the caterpillar's own material, using waiting cells. It gets wrong that real waiting cells grow from tiny to big, and that some parts are kept, not broken down.
items.why: Every model is useful but not perfect. Saying what it gets wrong is part of thinking like a scientist.
items.context: In Rebuild the Body, you made a dough caterpillar with folded papers inside, then rebuilt it into a butterfly.

items.p: Draw a mosquito's life cycle: egg, wriggler, tumbler, adult. Show which stages live in water.
items.a: Eggs on the water, a wriggler hanging under the surface, a curled tumbler in the water, and a flying adult. The first three are in water.
items.why: Three of the four stages live in water. That is why tipping out still water stops mosquitoes.
items.context: In the Wriggler Check, you looked for mosquito babies in still water at home.

worksheets.context: This worksheet goes further: moulting, eggs, hormones, the tadpole's tail and how different insects grow up.

worksheets.title: Big Changes, Big Questions (challenge)

items.p: In 1912, Friedrich Gudernatsch fed tadpoles a little dried thyroid. What happened?
opts: They turned into tiny frogs much too early
items.why: The thyroid makes the hormone that switches on metamorphosis. Extra hormone made the change start early. Picking 'giant tadpoles' is close to the opposite result. Tadpoles without a thyroid stay tadpoles and keep growing.

items.p: Francesco Redi covered some jars of meat with thin cloth, and left others open. Maggots grew only in the open jars. What did this show?
opts: Maggots come from eggs laid by flies, not from the meat
items.why: Flies could not reach the covered meat, so they couldn't lay eggs there. So maggots must come from fly eggs. Picking 'cloth stops meat going bad' misses the point. The covered meat still went bad, it just had no maggots.

items.p: Why might it help a frog that their tadpoles live in water and eat slime, while adult frogs live on land and eat insects?
opts: The young and adults don't compete for the same food
items.why: When the young and the adults eat different food in different places, they don't take food from each other. This is one idea for why metamorphosis is useful. No one can go back in time to check how it began. 'Frogs cannot swim' is false, because frogs swim well.

items.p: In 2008, scientists taught moth caterpillars to stay away from one smell. Many of the adult moths still stayed away from it. What might this mean?
items.why: It suggests that some part of what the caterpillar learned passes through the pupa. Other scientists want more tests before they are sure. Picking 'the caterpillars never changed' can't be right, because they became moths with wings.

items.p: Which came first, the chicken or the egg?
opts: The egg. Animals laid eggs for hundreds of millions of years before there were chickens.
The chicken, because something must lay the egg
Nobody could ever have any idea
items.why: Fish, early amphibians and reptiles laid eggs long before chickens existed. Chickens come from red junglefowl, which also lay eggs. So eggs came first. Picking 'the chicken' makes sense only if you mean a chicken's egg. Even then, the first chicken hatched from an egg laid by a bird that was almost a chicken.

items.p: Look at this caterpillar diary chart. About how many times longer was the caterpillar on day 16 than on day 2?
items.why: On day 2 they were 4 millimetres. On day 16 they were 40 millimetres. 40 divided by 4 is 10. Picking 36 means subtracting, 40 minus 4, which tells you how much they grew, not how many times longer they are.
items.context: In Raise a Lime Butterfly, you measured a caterpillar every day. These numbers are made up, to show what a diary might look like.

items.p: Some frogs in the Western Ghats hatch straight out of the egg as tiny froglets, with no tadpole stage.
items.why: True. Some bush frogs lay their eggs on land, on leaves or moss. The tadpole stage happens inside the egg, and a tiny froglet hatches.

items.p: All the atoms in a butterfly's body are brand new and have never been part of anything else.
items.why: False. The caterpillar built their body from leaves, and the leaves were built from air, water and soil. Atoms go round and round, through plants, animals, soil and air.

items.p: Your thyroid makes a hormone of the same kind as a tadpole's.
items.why: True. Your thyroid makes the same kind of hormone. It helps you grow and use energy. It needs iodine, which is why salt in India has iodine added.

items.p: The small groups of cells inside a caterpillar that wait, then grow into wings, legs and eyes, are called ____ discs.
items.why: Imaginal discs. 'Imago' is the old scientific word for an adult insect.

items.p: A moth caterpillar spins a silk case called a ____. A butterfly pupa is called a ____.
items.why: A cocoon is made of silk spun by a moth caterpillar. A chrysalis is the hard skin of a butterfly pupa.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Butterfly, mosquito, honeybee, grasshopper.
items.why: The grasshopper is the odd one out. They have no pupa. Their nymphs look like small adults. The other three have four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult.

items.p: A frog lays hundreds of eggs, but only a few become frogs. A hen lays fewer eggs and looks after her chicks. Give one good thing about each way.
items.a: Lots of eggs: even if most are eaten, a few will survive, and the parent doesn't need to stay. Fewer eggs with care: each chick has a much better chance, because the hen keeps them warm and safe.
items.why: Both ways work, in different lives. Scientists compare these two ways: many young with no care, or a few young with lots of care.

items.p: Silk is made from silkworm cocoons. Usually the pupa inside is killed so the thread stays in one long piece. Some people make 'peace silk', where the moth comes out first. What do you think, and why?
items.a: Any honest, thought-out answer is good. For example: I think peace silk is kinder, because the moth gets to finish their life cycle, even if the thread is shorter.
items.why: This is a question about fairness, not a fact. The best answers say what they think and give a reason.

items.p: In the story 'Where the Tails Go', Kavya thought her tadpoles were sick. Her friend Farida's notebook showed something else. Why are written records useful in science?
items.a: Memory can trick us, and worry can make us see things. The notebook showed the tail shrinking a little each day, not snapping. That pattern told them it was being taken back in.
items.why: Scientists measure and write things down, so that they can see patterns they would otherwise miss.

items.p: Your body is slowly rebuilt from the food you eat. Is the rice you ate today going to be part of you? Explain.
items.a: Yes. My body breaks down food and uses some of it to build new cells, like skin, blood and muscle. So some of today's rice will become part of me.
items.why: Like a tadpole using their tail, or a chick using their yolk, your body takes food apart and builds with the pieces. Every living thing does this.

items.p: Draw a waiting cell inside a caterpillar, and then draw what it becomes inside the chrysalis.
items.a: A tiny flat patch of cells inside the caterpillar, then a big wing inside the chrysalis.
items.why: The wing was there all along as a tiny flat pocket of cells, waiting. In the chrysalis, it grows fast using the caterpillar's material.

items.p: Label the parts of the egg in the picture: shell, skin, air pocket, white, twisted cord, yolk.
items.a: Shell on the outside, skin just inside it, air pocket at the round end, white around the yolk, twisted cords on each side of the yolk, yolk in the middle.
items.why: Each part has a job. Together they keep the chick fed, cushioned and breathing for 21 days.
