experiments.title: Can an egg breathe? Bubbles from a shell
experiments.question: Can air get in and out through an eggshell?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. We will put one egg in very hot water and one in cold water. Will anything come out of the shells? Will it come from the round end, the pointed end, or all over? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use two eggs from the same box, two glasses the same size and the same amount of water. Only the warmth of the water changes. Watch each egg for the same time, one minute.
results_table: Trails of bubbles from the round half in 1 minute
Trails of bubbles from the pointed half in 1 minute

materials.item: raw eggs from the same box, straight from the fridge if you keep them there
clear glasses or jars, big enough to cover an egg with water
very hot water: 2 cups of just-boiled water mixed with 1 cup of tap water
cold water from the tap
a spoon, to lower the eggs in
a magnifying glass, if you have one

experiments.safety: A grown-up mixes and pours the hot water. It should be very hot but not boiling. Lift the eggs out with a spoon, and let them cool before anyone holds them.

schedule.what: Guess. Put one egg in very hot water and one in cold water. Watch for bubbles. Count the trails from each end. Write it down.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw your egg and mark where the bubbles came out.
experiments.context: This experiment tests whether air can pass through an eggshell. You put one egg in very hot water and one in cold water, and look for bubbles.

setup.art: Two clear glasses side by side, one labelled 'hot' with a little steam, one labelled 'cold', each with a whole raw egg at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Put one egg in each glass. A grown-up pours very hot water over one. Pour cold water over the other.

setup.art: Close-up of an egg in hot water with thin trails of tiny bubbles rising from its shell, more at the round end than the pointed end.
setup.caption: 2. Watch the shell closely for one minute.

setup.art: A child making tally marks on paper next to the two glasses.
setup.caption: 3. Count the trails of bubbles from each end. Write the numbers down.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: trails of bubbles counted in 1 minute
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: 1. Give your child a raw egg. 2. Ask them to look closely at the shell, with a magnifying glass if you have one.
flow.say: A chick grows inside an egg for three weeks. They need to breathe the whole time. But the shell looks solid. How could air get in?
flow.kid: Look closely at an eggshell. Can you see any holes? A chick inside needs air. How could they breathe?

ask.q: How do you think a chick breathes inside an egg?
good: There are tiny holes in the shell.
Air comes through the shell.
There is air inside the egg already.

flow.context: This is the first step of the eggshell bubbles experiment. You look closely at an eggshell and wonder how a chick breathes inside.
flow.parent: The holes are too small to see clearly, even with a magnifying glass. That is fine. The test will show whether they are there.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess, give a reason, and write the guess down.
flow.say: We will put one egg in very hot water and one in cold water. What do you think will happen to each egg? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. What will happen in hot water? In cold water? Why? Write your guess.

flow.do: 1. Lower one egg gently into each empty glass with a spoon. 2. Pour cold tap water over one egg until it is covered. 3. A grown-up pours the very hot water over the other egg until it is covered.
flow.say: Now we watch very closely. Don't touch the glasses. Just look at the shell.
flow.kid: Watch the shells. Don't touch the glasses. What do you see?
flow.parent: In very hot water, thin trails of tiny bubbles rise from the shell within a few seconds. There are usually more at the fat, round end, where the air pocket is. In cold water there are usually none. If you see only a few bubbles, the water was not hot enough. Try again with hotter water. If a shell cracks and white leaks out, use another egg.

flow.do: 1. On the hot egg, count the trails of bubbles from the round half for one minute. 2. Then count the trails from the pointed half. 3. Look at the cold egg. 4. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Let's count the thin lines of bubbles. Each line is coming out of one tiny hole, or a few. Make a tally mark for each line.
flow.kid: Count the lines of bubbles at the round end. Make tally marks. Now count at the pointed end. Then look at the cold egg.

check.q: In the eggshell test, bubbles came out of the egg in very hot water. What does this show?
options: The shell has tiny holes that let air through
Water is getting into the egg and pushing out bubbles
check.why: The heat makes the air inside the egg swell. It pushes out through thousands of tiny holes in the shell. The same holes let fresh air in for a growing chick. Picking 'the egg is boiling' usually means thinking bubbles always mean boiling. But the water is not boiling, and the bubbles come from the shell, not the water.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why did it happen?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: an eggshell has tiny holes that let air through. What I saw: in hot water, about 17 lines of bubbles came from the round half and 6 from the pointed half. In cold water there were none. Why: the heat made the air inside swell and push out through the holes. There is an air pocket at the round end, so more came out there. A chick breathes through the same holes.
flow.think: A hen's eggshell has thousands of tiny holes. Why don't germs and water get in more easily? Hint: there is a thin skin under the shell.

experiments.title: The Naked Egg: what is under the shell?
experiments.question: What holds an egg together if the shell is taken away?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If vinegar takes away the shell, will the egg spill out? Will it get bigger, smaller or stay the same size? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Measure the egg the same way each time. Wrap the string around the fattest part, mark it, and measure the string against a ruler.
results_table: Does it bounce if dropped 2 cm onto a tray? (yes or no)

materials.item: a raw egg
white vinegar, enough to cover the egg
a glass jar with a lid
a piece of string and a ruler, or a soft measuring tape
a torch

experiments.safety: Vinegar stings in eyes and cuts, so wash hands after touching it. Handle the naked egg over a sink or tray. Throw the egg away at the end. Do not eat it.

schedule.what: Measure the egg. Put it in a jar of vinegar. Watch the bubbles.
Look at the egg. Pour away the old vinegar and add fresh vinegar.
Rinse the naked egg. Measure it. Shine a torch through it. Gently test its bounce.

experiments.record: Fill in the table each day. Draw the egg on Day 1 and on Day 3.
experiments.context: In this experiment, vinegar slowly takes away an egg's shell over two days. You find out what is underneath.

setup.art: A child wrapping a string round the middle of an egg, and a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Measure around the fattest part of the egg with a string.

setup.art: An egg sitting at the bottom of a glass jar of vinegar, covered with tiny bubbles.
setup.caption: 2. Put the egg in a jar and cover it with vinegar. Watch the bubbles.

setup.art: A see-through, rubbery egg glowing orange as a torch shines through it in a dark room.
setup.caption: 3. After two days, rinse it. Shine a torch through it. Measure it again.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: distance around the egg
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your egg may grow a little more or a little less.

flow.do: 1. Wrap the string round the fattest part of the egg. 2. Pinch where it meets. 3. Lay the string along the ruler and write the number in the table.
flow.say: An eggshell is hard. But what is underneath? Vinegar slowly eats away eggshell. Let's measure our egg first, so we can see if it changes.
flow.kid: Wrap a string round the fat middle of the egg. Pinch it. Measure the string with a ruler. Write the number.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Naked Egg experiment. You measure an egg before vinegar takes away its shell.

flow.do: 1. Put the egg gently in the jar. 2. Pour in vinegar until the egg is covered. 3. Watch for two minutes. 4. Put the lid on loosely.
flow.say: Look at the shell. Tiny bubbles are growing on it. What do you think is happening?
flow.kid: Put the egg in the jar. Cover it with vinegar. Watch the shell. What do you see?

ask.q: What is happening on the shell?
good: Bubbles are coming out.
The vinegar is eating the shell.
It is fizzing.

flow.parent: The shell is mostly calcium carbonate, the same material as chalk and limestone. Vinegar breaks it down, and the bubbles are carbon dioxide gas. Keep the lid loose so the gas can escape.

flow.do: Look at the egg. Pour the old vinegar down the sink, holding the egg back with a spoon. Add fresh vinegar.
flow.say: Look, some of the shell has gone already. Let's give it fresh vinegar so it can finish.
flow.kid: Day 2. Look at your egg. Is the shell going? Pour away the old vinegar. Add new vinegar.

flow.do: 1. Lift the egg out with a spoon and rinse it gently under the tap. 2. Rub off any leftover shell. 3. Measure it with the string again. 4. In a dark room, shine a torch through it. 5. Drop it from 2 cm, about the width of two fingers, onto a tray.
flow.say: The shell is gone. What is holding the egg together now? Gently feel it. Now let's shine a light through it.
flow.kid: Rinse your egg. Feel it gently. Measure it again. Shine a torch through it. Can you see the yolk?
flow.parent: The egg is held together by its two thin skins, the membranes. It is usually a little bigger, because water from the vinegar soaks in through the skins. With the torch you can often see the yolk as a dark shadow.

check.q: In the Naked Egg experiment, the shell is gone but the egg does not spill. What holds it together?
options: Two thin skins under the shell
check.why: Under the shell are two thin, strong skins called membranes. They hold the egg in a bag shape even without the shell. Picking 'the yolk' usually means thinking the yolk holds the egg. But the yolk is a ball of food floating inside.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Then throw the egg away and wash hands.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why did it happen?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: an egg has a skin under its shell that holds it together. What I saw: after two days in vinegar the shell was gone, but the egg stayed whole and bounced a little. It also grew from 14 to 15 centimetres around. Why: the vinegar broke down the shell, but not the skins. Water soaked in through the skins, so the egg got bigger.
flow.think: The shell keeps the chick safe, and the skins keep germs out. What else in nature has a hard outside and a soft skin inside?

experiments.title: Tadpole Watch: where does the tail go? (if you live near a pond in the monsoon)
experiments.question: As a tadpole becomes a frog, which legs come first, and does their tail fall off or shrink a little each day?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the back legs or the front legs come first? Will the tail drop off in one go, or get shorter slowly? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Measure the same way each time. Hold the ruler outside the jar, level with the tadpole, and measure from the nose to where the tail starts, then the tail. Measure every second day, at about the same time.

materials.item: a wide plastic tub or bucket, about 5 litres
pond water from the same puddle, never tap water
materials.qty: enough to fill the tub halfway

materials.item: a stone with green slime on it, and a few water plants
3 to 5 tadpoles from a monsoon puddle that is drying up
a little boiled and cooled spinach
a ruler in millimetres
a magnifying glass

experiments.safety: A grown-up comes to the pond and collects the tadpoles. Wash hands after touching pond water. Keep the tub in shade, never in hot sun. Put a stone or a stick in, so froglets can climb out. Take every animal back to the same pond when they have legs. Do this only in the monsoon, from a temporary puddle, and only with common frogs or toads.

schedule.what: Collect 3 to 5 tadpoles with a grown-up. Set up the tub. Measure each tadpole. Start the table.
Measure the tadpoles and write the numbers. Give a pinch of spinach. Do this every second day.
Look closely for back legs with the magnifying glass.
Look for front legs. Are the tadpoles still eating?
Measure the tails as they shrink. Make sure froglets can climb out of the water.
Carry the froglets back to their pond. Draw the line chart of tail length.

experiments.record: Fill in the table every second day. At the end, draw a line chart of tail length against day.
experiments.context: This is a six-week monsoon experiment for families who live near a pond, a paddy field or a big rain puddle. You keep a few tadpoles in pond water, measure them every second day, and find out what happens to the tail.

setup.art: A grown-up and a child at the edge of a muddy monsoon puddle, scooping tadpoles gently with a steel tumbler.
setup.caption: 1. With a grown-up, scoop 3 to 5 tadpoles from a drying puddle.

setup.art: A wide tub in the shade with pond water, a slimy stone, some water weeds and a stick leaning on the side.
setup.caption: 2. Set up a tub with pond water, a slimy stone and a stick to climb.

setup.art: A child holding a ruler against the outside of a clear tub, level with a tadpole, and writing in a notebook.
setup.caption: 3. Every second day, measure the body and the tail. Write it down.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: one tadpole's tail length
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your tadpoles will change at their own speed.

flow.do: 1. With your child, find a monsoon puddle with tadpoles that may dry up. 2. Fill the tub halfway with water from that puddle. 3. Add a slimy stone, a few weeds and a stick. 4. Scoop 3 to 5 tadpoles gently in a tumbler and pour them in. 5. Keep the tub in the shade.
flow.say: These tadpoles are going to become frogs. We'll look after a few for some weeks, and then bring them all back here. We are borrowing them, not keeping them.
flow.kid: With a grown-up, scoop a few tadpoles into pond water. Add a slimy stone and a stick. Keep it in the shade. You are borrowing them.
flow.context: This is the first step of Tadpole Watch. You collect a few tadpoles and set up a home for them in pond water.
flow.parent: Use only pond water. Tap water has chlorine, which can harm tadpoles. Five tadpoles in 5 litres is plenty, because more will dirty the water. If you cannot find tadpoles, watch the tadpole video in this unit instead, and read the story 'Where the Tails Go'.

flow.do: 1. Hold the ruler outside the tub, level with one tadpole. 2. Measure their body, from nose to the start of the tail. 3. Measure their tail. 4. Write both numbers. 5. Do the same for each tadpole. 6. Drop in a pinch of spinach.
flow.say: Measure gently, from outside. We don't need to touch them.
flow.kid: Hold the ruler outside the tub. Measure the body. Measure the tail. Write the numbers. Give a pinch of spinach.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Look with a magnifying glass at the place where the body meets the tail.
flow.say: Look closely where the tail starts. Can you see two tiny bumps? Those are the first legs.
flow.kid: Look where the tail starts. Can you see two tiny bumps? Those are legs!

check.q: In Tadpole Watch, which legs does a tadpole grow first?
options: All four at the same time
check.why: The back legs grow first, near the tail. The front legs grow hidden under the skin, and pop out later. Picking 'front legs' is a natural guess, because the front is where the head is. Picking 'all four' usually means you haven't seen the front legs hiding yet.

flow.do: When front legs appear, check every day. Notice whether the tadpoles eat the spinach. Make sure the stick is there so froglets can climb out.
flow.say: Watch the tail now. Is it snapping off, or getting shorter a little each day? And are they still eating?
flow.kid: Front legs! Now watch the tail. Is it getting shorter? Are they eating?
flow.parent: Tadpoles usually stop eating while the tail shrinks. Don't worry. Their mouth and gut are being rebuilt, and they live on the material of their own tail. The froglets must be able to climb out, or they can drown, because they now breathe air.

check.q: In Tadpole Watch, the tails got shorter a little each day, and the tadpoles stopped eating. Why?
options: The tail is broken down and used as food for building the frog
check.why: The tail cells break down on purpose. The body uses that material to build legs, lungs and a new mouth. So the tadpole doesn't need to eat for a while. Picking 'sick' is a common worry, because a hungry animal that won't eat usually is sick. Picking 'biting' fits a tail that seems to vanish, but you would see bite marks and bits on the bottom.

flow.do: 1. When each froglet has only a tiny tail stub, carry the tub to the pond. 2. Tip the froglets gently onto the mud at the edge. 3. At home, draw a line chart of one tadpole's tail length.
flow.say: They're ready. Let's take them home. Then we'll make a picture of what happened to the tail.
flow.kid: Take your froglets back to their pond. Let them hop away. Then draw a line chart of tail length.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think happens to a tadpole's tail? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the tail doesn't fall off, it goes into the body. What I saw: the tail grew to 18 millimetres, then shrank a little every day, to 8 and then 2. We never found a tail in the tub, and the tadpoles stopped eating. Why: the body breaks the tail down and uses it to build the frog.

activities.title: Open an Egg like a Scientist

materials.item: a raw egg
a white plate or a steel thali
a magnifying glass
a spoon and a toothpick
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Wash hands with soap after touching raw egg. Use the egg for cooking afterwards, or throw it away.

schedule.what: Crack an egg onto a plate. Find all its parts. Draw and label them.

activities.record: Draw the egg on the plate. Label the yolk, the white, the twisted cords, the white spot, the skins and the air pocket.
activities.context: This activity opens a hen's egg so you can find every part a growing chick would need. It is a good way to start the unit.

setup.art: A child holding an egg up to a window and looking at the shell through a magnifying glass.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the shell first. Which end is round and which is pointed?

setup.art: An egg cracked onto a white plate, showing the yellow yolk, clear white, two white twisted cords and a tiny white spot on the yolk.
setup.caption: 2. Crack the egg gently onto a white plate.

setup.art: The inside of an empty half eggshell at its round end, with a thin skin peeled back to show a small air pocket.
setup.caption: 3. Look inside the round end of the shell for the air pocket.

flow.do: 1. Give your child a raw egg. 2. Ask them to look at it with a magnifying glass and say what they notice.
flow.say: This egg came from a hen. If a rooster had mated with the hen, an egg like this could grow a chick. Look closely. What do you notice? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Look at the egg with a magnifying glass. What do you notice? What do you wonder about?

ask.q: What do you notice about the shell?
good: It has tiny dots.
One end is fatter.
It feels a bit rough.

flow.context: This is the first step of Open an Egg like a Scientist. You look closely at a hen's egg before you crack it.

flow.do: 1. Tap the middle of the egg on the edge of the plate. 2. Open it gently with both thumbs, close to the plate, so the yolk doesn't break. 3. Keep both halves of the shell.
flow.say: Let's open it gently, like a doctor, so we don't break anything inside.
flow.kid: Tap the egg on the plate edge. Open it gently with two thumbs. Keep both halves of the shell.

flow.do: Find each part with your child. Point with the toothpick. Name it and say its job.
flow.say: The yellow ball is the yolk. It is the chick's food. The clear part is the white. It holds water and cushions the yolk. These two white twisted cords are like ropes holding the yolk in the middle. Can you find a tiny white spot on top of the yolk?
flow.kid: Find the yellow yolk. It's food for a chick. Find the clear white. It holds water. Find the two twisted cords. Look for a tiny white spot on the yolk.
flow.parent: The white spot is called the germinal disc. A chick would begin there if the egg were fertilised. Most shop eggs are not fertilised, so it stays a spot. The twisted cords are called chalazae. Some people think they are the start of a chick, but they only hold the yolk in place.

check.q: In the egg on the plate, which part is food for a growing chick?
check.why: The yolk is a big ball of food. A growing chick slowly uses it up over 21 days. Picking 'the twisted cords' is a common mix-up. They look a bit like something alive, but they are just ropes that hold the yolk in the middle.

flow.do: 1. Look inside the round end of the empty shell. 2. Peel back the thin skin with a fingernail. 3. Find the small hollow where the air pocket was.
flow.say: Under the shell there are two thin skins. At the round end, they come apart and leave a pocket of air. Just before hatching, the chick pokes their beak into this pocket and takes their first breath.
flow.kid: Look inside the round end of the shell. Peel the thin skin. Find the little pocket where air was. A chick takes their first breath here.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the egg and label six parts: shell, skin, air pocket, white, cords and yolk with its spot.
flow.say: Draw what you found, like a scientist. Label every part, and write one job next to each.
flow.kid: Draw your egg. Label the parts. Write one job for each part.
flow.think: Everything a chick needs for three weeks is inside this egg, except two things. What comes in from outside? Hint: think about air and warmth.

activities.title: Three Life Cycle Wheels

materials.item: three paper plates
three split pins, or three thumb pins pushed through a small piece of eraser behind the plate
card for the pointers
crayons or colour pencils
a ruler

activities.safety: A grown-up pushes the split pins through the plates.

schedule.what: Make a frog wheel, a butterfly wheel and a hen wheel. Spin each one and tell its story.

activities.record: Your three wheels are the record. On the back of each, write how many stages it has.
activities.context: In this activity you make three spinning paper-plate wheels, one each for the life cycles of a frog, a butterfly and a hen.

setup.art: A paper plate with pencil lines dividing it into four equal parts.
setup.caption: 1. Draw lines to split each plate into parts: four for the frog and butterfly, three for the hen.

setup.art: A child colouring an egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and butterfly into the four parts of a plate.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one stage in each part, going clockwise.

setup.art: Three finished plates with card arrows pinned in the middle, one frog, one butterfly, one hen.
setup.caption: 3. Pin an arrow in the middle. Spin it and tell the story.

flow.do: 1. On two plates, draw two lines across the middle to make four parts. 2. On the third plate, draw three lines from the middle, like the letter Y, to make three parts.
flow.say: We'll make three wheels. The frog and butterfly have four stages. The hen has only three. Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Make four parts on two plates. Make three parts on the third plate. Which animal gets three?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Life Cycle Wheels activity. You split three paper plates into parts, one part for each stage.

flow.do: Help your child draw one stage in each part, going round like a clock. Butterfly: egg on a leaf, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly. Frog: frogspawn, tadpole, froglet, frog. Hen: egg, chick, hen.
flow.say: Draw them going round like the hands of a clock. Draw arrows from each stage to the next. What comes after the last one?
flow.kid: Draw one stage in each part. Go round like a clock. Draw arrows. After the last stage, the arrow goes back to the first!

check.q: On the butterfly wheel, which stage comes between the caterpillar and the butterfly?
check.why: The caterpillar makes a chrysalis, and the butterfly comes out of it. Picking 'egg' usually means thinking the butterfly hatches straight from an egg, like a chick. A tadpole belongs to the frog's wheel.

flow.do: 1. Cut three arrows from card. 2. A grown-up pins one in the middle of each plate. 3. Your child spins each and tells the story.
flow.say: Spin the arrow. Wherever it stops, tell me what this animal is doing and what happens next.
flow.kid: Spin the arrow. Where did it stop? Say what the animal does now, and what comes next.

ask.q: Why does the hen wheel have fewer parts?
good: The chick already looks like a hen.
They don't change shape, they just grow.
There is no tadpole or caterpillar stage.

activities.title: Be a Caterpillar, Be a Butterfly

materials.item: a bedsheet or an old sari
some space on the floor

activities.safety: Keep the sheet loose around the body, never over the face.

schedule.what: Act out a butterfly's life, from egg to flying, as the parent reads.

activities.record: Draw yourself in your favourite stage.
activities.context: This is an acting activity. The child acts out each stage of a butterfly's life with their whole body, while the parent reads.

setup.art: A child curled up small on the floor like an egg.
setup.caption: 1. Curl up small like an egg on a leaf.

setup.art: A child crawling on the floor, pretending to munch a cushion like a leaf.
setup.caption: 2. Crawl and munch like a caterpillar.

setup.art: A child wrapped loosely in an old sari up to the shoulders, standing very still, then opening arms wide like wings.
setup.caption: 3. Wrap up still as a chrysalis, then open your wings.

flow.do: Your child curls up small on the floor.
flow.say: You are a tiny egg on a curry leaf. Your mother chose this plant, because you will be able to eat their leaves. Stay very still. Inside you, a caterpillar is growing.
flow.kid: Curl up very small. You are an egg on a leaf. Stay still. Something is growing inside you.
flow.context: This is the first step of an acting game. Your child becomes a butterfly egg, then grows through every stage.

flow.do: Your child crawls, munching cushions like leaves. Every so often, call out 'Too tight!' and they wriggle out of an imaginary skin.
flow.say: You hatch! First, eat your eggshell. Now eat leaves. Eat and eat. Your skin is getting too tight. Wriggle out of it! You are bigger now. Eat more.
flow.kid: Hatch! Eat your eggshell. Crawl and munch leaves. Your skin is tight! Wriggle out of it. Keep eating.

check.q: Why does a caterpillar wriggle out of their skin?
options: Their old skin is too tight because they have grown
They are turning into a butterfly already
check.why: A caterpillar's skin does not stretch much. So they grow a new, bigger skin underneath and wriggle out of the old one. This is called moulting. Picking 'turning into a butterfly' mixes up moulting with metamorphosis. A caterpillar moults several times and is still a caterpillar.

flow.do: Wrap the sari loosely round your child up to the shoulders. They stand very still for one minute.
flow.say: Now stop eating. Hang still. You are a chrysalis. From the outside, nothing is happening. Inside, your body is being rebuilt. Waiting cells are growing wings. Stay still and feel your wings growing.
flow.kid: Stop eating. Stand very still. You are a chrysalis. Inside, your body is being rebuilt. Feel your wings growing.
flow.parent: Count slowly to 60 together. Children find stillness hard, which makes the point. The chrysalis is the busiest stage, even though it looks like nothing is happening.

flow.do: Your child wriggles out of the sari, stands, and slowly spreads their arms.
flow.say: Split your case! Climb out. Your wings are crumpled and wet. Pump them slowly. Wait for them to dry. Now fly, find a flower, and drink.
flow.kid: Break out! Your wings are wet and crumpled. Open them slowly. Now fly to a flower.
flow.think: Were you the same you all the way through, egg to butterfly?

activities.title: Rebuild the Body: from caterpillar to butterfly

materials.item: a ball of dough about the size of an orange: atta mixed with a little water and salt, or play dough
four small pieces of paper, folded tiny

schedule.what: Build a caterpillar, break it down, and rebuild a butterfly from the same material.

activities.record: Draw the caterpillar, the ball and the butterfly. Write: 'The butterfly was built from the caterpillar.'
activities.context: This activity is a hands-on model of metamorphosis. You make a dough caterpillar with tiny folded papers inside, then squash it and rebuild a butterfly from the same dough.

setup.art: A child pressing four tiny folded paper squares into a long dough caterpillar.
setup.caption: 1. Make a dough caterpillar. Hide four tiny folded papers inside: the waiting cells.

setup.art: The dough squashed into a ball, with the four folded papers still whole inside it.
setup.caption: 2. Squash it into a ball: the chrysalis. Keep the papers whole.

setup.art: A dough butterfly with four paper wings unfolded and stuck into its sides.
setup.caption: 3. Unfold the papers into wings. Build the butterfly from the same dough.

flow.do: 1. Your child rolls the dough into a long caterpillar. 2. Fold four small papers very tiny. 3. Press them inside the caterpillar, two on each side.
flow.say: These tiny papers stand for special cells. They have been inside the caterpillar since they hatched, waiting. Scientists call them imaginal discs. 'Imago' is the old word for an adult insect.
flow.kid: Roll the dough into a caterpillar. Fold four papers very small. Hide them inside. They are waiting cells. They will become wings.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rebuild the Body activity. You make a dough caterpillar with tiny folded papers hidden inside as waiting cells.

flow.do: Your child squashes the caterpillar into a ball, carefully keeping the four papers whole.
flow.say: Now the caterpillar has become a chrysalis. Inside, most of their body is broken down. But the waiting cells stay whole. Squash the dough, but keep the papers safe.
flow.kid: Squash the caterpillar into a ball. That is the chrysalis. Keep the papers whole inside. They are the waiting cells.

flow.do: 1. Find the four papers. 2. Unfold them into wings. 3. Shape the dough into a butterfly body, with a head, six legs and two feelers. 4. Stick the wings on.
flow.say: The waiting cells grow fast. They use the broken-down caterpillar as building material. Use all the dough. Nothing is thrown away.
flow.kid: Find the papers. Unfold them into wings. Make a butterfly body from all the dough. Use it all.

check.q: In the dough model, where did the butterfly's body come from?
options: From new dough added from outside
The butterfly was hiding inside, already made
check.why: Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar's body is broken down. The waiting cells build the butterfly out of that material. Picking 'hiding inside, already made' is a very old idea. People used to think a tiny butterfly was folded up inside every caterpillar, ready made. In fact only the waiting cells are there, and they must grow.

flow.do: Talk about what the model gets right and what it gets wrong.
flow.say: Our model is a bit like the real thing. But in a real chrysalis, some parts of the caterpillar, like bits of the nerves, are kept and changed, not broken down. What else might our model get wrong?
flow.kid: Is our model just like a real chrysalis? What is different? Say one thing.

ask.q: What does the dough model get wrong?
good: Real waiting cells grow, they don't just unfold.
A real chrysalis keeps some parts.
Real wings are made of cells, not paper.
It takes about two weeks, not one minute.

flow.think: Your body is also slowly rebuilt from the food you eat. Is the food you eat today going to be part of you?

activities.title: Curry Leaf Hunt: find a lime butterfly family

materials.item: a curry leaf, lemon or orange plant, in a pot, a garden or a park
a magnifying glass
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up comes along outside. Look, don't touch. If a caterpillar shows two orange horns, they are defending themself with a smell. Leave them in peace.

schedule.what: Search a curry leaf or lemon plant for eggs, caterpillars and chrysalises. Draw what you find.

activities.record: Draw each thing you find, and write where on the plant it was: top of a leaf, under a leaf, or on a stem.
activities.context: This is an outdoor hunt for the lime butterfly, a common Indian butterfly. She lays her eggs on curry leaf, lemon and orange plants.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up bending over a potted curry leaf plant on a balcony, the child holding a magnifying glass.
setup.caption: 1. Find a curry leaf, lemon or orange plant.

setup.art: Close-up of a fresh curry leaf tip with a tiny round pale-yellow egg on it.
setup.caption: 2. Look at the newest, softest leaves for tiny round eggs.

setup.art: A small brown-and-white caterpillar on a leaf that looks just like a bird dropping.
setup.caption: 3. Look for 'bird droppings' that are really caterpillars.

flow.do: Go outside with your child to a curry leaf, lemon or orange plant.
flow.say: A butterfly called the lime butterfly chooses these plants for her babies. Her caterpillars can only eat leaves from this plant family. Let's see if a mother has been here.
flow.kid: Find a curry leaf or lemon plant with a grown-up. A lime butterfly lays eggs here. Let's look.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Curry Leaf Hunt. You go outside to look for lime butterfly eggs and caterpillars.

flow.do: Search slowly, leaf by leaf. Look at the newest leaves at the tips, and under them. Use the magnifying glass.
flow.say: Look for three things. Tiny round eggs, like yellow mustard seeds. Small brown-and-white caterpillars that look like bird droppings. And bigger, fat green caterpillars.
flow.kid: Look slowly. Find tiny round eggs on new leaves. Find brown-and-white bird droppings. Some are caterpillars! Find fat green ones too.
flow.parent: If you find a 'bird dropping' that is shiny and has a shape, that is likely a young lime caterpillar. If you find nothing, that is a real result too. Try again in a week, especially after rain.

check.q: On the Curry Leaf Hunt, why does a young lime caterpillar look like a bird dropping?
options: So birds don't want to eat them
check.why: Birds eat caterpillars, but they don't eat bird droppings. Looking like a dropping keeps the young caterpillar safe. Picking 'dirty' or 'sick' means judging by how they look to us. To a bird, that look means 'not food'.

flow.do: Count how many eggs, caterpillars and chrysalises you find. Write the numbers.
flow.say: Let's count. Scientists always count. How many of each did we find?
flow.kid: Count the eggs. Count the caterpillars. Count any chrysalises. Write the numbers.

flow.do: Ask why the butterfly chooses this plant.
flow.say: Why did the mother butterfly lay her eggs here and not on the mango tree next door?
flow.kid: Why did the mother pick this plant? Say your idea.

ask.q: Why does the butterfly lay eggs only on certain plants?
good: Her caterpillars can only eat those leaves.
So the babies have food as soon as they hatch.
She can't feed them herself.

flow.think: A butterfly mother never meets her babies. How does she still look after them?

activities.title: Wriggler Check: find and stop mosquito babies

materials.item: a torch
a clear glass and a spoon
a list of places where water collects at home

activities.safety: A grown-up comes along. Wash hands after touching standing water. Never drink it.

schedule.what: Check pots, coolers and containers for wrigglers. Look at one in a glass. Tip the water out.

activities.record: Make a list of every place you checked. Write yes or no for wrigglers. Write what you did.
activities.context: This activity looks for mosquito larvae, called wrigglers, in standing water around the home. Mosquitoes have a four-stage life cycle, and stopping them at the wriggler stage protects people from dengue and malaria.

setup.art: A child shining a torch into the water of a plant pot saucer on a balcony.
setup.caption: 1. Shine a torch into every place where water stands still.

setup.art: A clear glass with a little water and several thin wrigglers hanging head-down from the surface.
setup.caption: 2. Scoop some water into a glass. Look for wrigglers.

setup.art: A child tipping water out of a saucer onto the soil while a grown-up scrubs it.
setup.caption: 3. Tip the water out and scrub the container.

flow.do: Check plant saucers, buckets, cooler trays, old tyres, coconut shells and flower vases with a torch.
flow.say: Mosquitoes lay their eggs in still water. Their babies live in the water for about a week before they fly. Let's check every place water stands still.
flow.kid: With a grown-up, shine a torch into still water. Check pots, buckets and coolers. Look for tiny wriggling things.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Wriggler Check. You look for mosquito babies in still water around the home.

flow.do: If you find wrigglers, scoop a spoonful into the glass. Look closely together.
flow.say: These are mosquito larvae, called wrigglers. They hang from the top of the water to breathe through a little tube. Curled ones, like commas, are the pupae, called tumblers. In a day or two they become mosquitoes.
flow.kid: Look at the wrigglers in the glass. They hang from the top to breathe. Can you find a curled one? That is a pupa.

check.q: In the Wriggler Check, why do wrigglers hang at the top of the water?
options: They breathe air through a little tube
They are catching food falling from above
They are trying to fly away
check.why: Wrigglers live in water but breathe air. They hang from the surface with a tiny breathing tube poking out. Picking 'trying to fly away' mixes up the larva with the adult. Only adult mosquitoes have wings.

flow.do: Tip the water out onto dry ground or into a pot of soil, never into a drain. Scrub the container. Turn buckets upside down.
flow.say: With no still water, mosquito eggs cannot grow into adults. That is how families and towns fight dengue and malaria. In 1897, in Secunderabad, a doctor named Ronald Ross found the malaria germ living inside mosquitoes.
flow.kid: Tip the water onto soil. Scrub the pot. Turn buckets upside down. You stopped a life cycle!
flow.parent: Doing this every week stops most home mosquito breeding, because the cycle from egg to adult takes about a week in warm weather. Scrubbing matters, because Aedes mosquito eggs stick to container walls and can survive drying.

projects.title: Raise a Lime Butterfly

materials.item: a lime butterfly egg or small caterpillar, found on a curry leaf or lemon plant
a mesh butterfly cage, or a big clear jar with cloth tied over the top
fresh curry leaf or lemon leaves, from the same kind of plant they were found on
a small jar of water to keep the sprig fresh, with cotton plugging the top
a ruler and a magnifying glass
a notebook for the diary

projects.safety: Keep the cage in the shade, not in the sun. Plug the water jar with cotton so the caterpillar cannot fall in and drown. Release the butterfly near the plant where you found them.

schedule.what: With a grown-up, collect an egg or a tiny caterpillar on their leaf. Set up the cage. Start the diary.
Every day: give fresh leaves, take out droppings, measure the caterpillar and write one line in the diary.
Look for an empty skin. Have they moulted? Are they green yet?
The caterpillar stops eating and wanders. Watch them tie themself to a stem with a silk belt.
Draw the chrysalis. Keep the cage still. Check it once a day.
The chrysalis turns dark and you can see wing colours. The butterfly comes out. Let them dry for a few hours, then release them.

projects.record: Keep a diary with one line and one number each day: the caterpillar's length in millimetres. At the end, make a line chart of their length.
projects.context: This is a four-week project. You raise a lime butterfly from an egg or a tiny caterpillar, keep a daily diary, and let the butterfly go.

setup.art: A mesh cage on a shady table with a sprig of curry leaves standing in a small cotton-plugged jar of water, and a small caterpillar on a leaf.
setup.caption: 1. Set up a cage with a fresh sprig of leaves in a plugged jar.

setup.art: A child measuring a green caterpillar on a leaf with a ruler held beside it, and writing in a diary.
setup.caption: 2. Every day, give fresh leaves, clean out droppings and measure.

setup.art: A lime butterfly with black and yellow wings resting on an empty chrysalis case, ready to fly.
setup.caption: 3. When the butterfly comes out and their wings are dry, let them go.

flow.do: 1. Find an egg or a tiny caterpillar on a curry leaf or lemon plant. 2. Snip the leaf with them. 3. Stand a fresh sprig in a small jar of water, plug the top with cotton, and put it in the cage. 4. Lay the snipped leaf on the sprig.
flow.say: We are going to borrow this baby butterfly for a few weeks, and watch their whole change. At the end, we'll let them go right here.
flow.kid: With a grown-up, find an egg or a tiny caterpillar. Put them with fresh leaves in a cage. You are borrowing them.
flow.context: This is the first step of Raise a Lime Butterfly. You find a young caterpillar and set up a home for them.
flow.parent: Look on the newest leaves of a curry leaf, lemon or orange plant. Nursery plants often carry eggs or tiny caterpillars. If you find none, try again after a week, or watch the butterfly video in this unit instead.

flow.do: Every day: 1. Put in a fresh sprig. 2. Shake out the droppings. 3. Hold a ruler beside the caterpillar without touching them. 4. Write their length and one thing you noticed.
flow.say: A caterpillar spends their days eating. Let's see how much they grow. Measure them every day, without touching.
flow.kid: Every day: fresh leaves, clean the cage, measure the caterpillar. Write one line in your diary.
flow.wait: Do this every day for about 18 days

chart.title: Made-up example: a few lines of a caterpillar diary
rows: Brown and white, like a bird dropping.
Found an empty skin. They are green now!
Fat and green. Eats a whole leaf in an hour.

flow.do: When you find a crumpled empty skin, look at it with the magnifying glass.
flow.say: Look, an old skin. The caterpillar grew a new, bigger skin underneath and wriggled out of this one. That is called moulting.
flow.kid: Find the empty skin. Look at it closely. Your caterpillar got too big for it!

check.q: In the butterfly diary, the caterpillar went from brown and white to green after a moult. Are they still a caterpillar?
options: Yes, they moulted but they are still a caterpillar
No, they are now a chrysalis
No, this is a different caterpillar
check.why: Moulting is shedding a skin to grow. A caterpillar moults four times and stays a caterpillar. Only their last moult makes the chrysalis. Picking 'a different caterpillar' is a fair guess, because they look so different. But you have watched them the whole time, so you know.

flow.do: When the caterpillar stops eating and wanders around the cage, watch closely. They will choose a stem and spin a silk belt.
flow.say: They have stopped eating. They're looking for a safe place. Watch them make a belt of silk around themself, like a seat belt.
flow.kid: Your caterpillar stopped eating. Watch them find a stem. They tie themself on with a silk belt!
flow.parent: Don't move the cage now. If the caterpillar falls, they can be hurt. In a day they will moult a last time, and the chrysalis will appear under the old skin.

flow.do: Draw the chrysalis every second day. Notice its colour. Do not touch it.
flow.say: It looks like nothing is happening. But inside, the caterpillar's body is being broken down, and their waiting cells are building wings, legs and eyes.
flow.kid: Draw the chrysalis. Don't touch it. Inside, wings are being built.

flow.do: 1. When the chrysalis turns dark and you see wing colours, check it often. 2. Watch the butterfly come out. 3. Wait 2 to 3 hours for their wings to dry. 4. Take the cage to the plant and open it.
flow.say: Here they come. Their wings are soft and crumpled. They are pumping blood into them. Don't help them. They need to do this themself to make their wings strong.
flow.kid: The butterfly is coming out! Watch them pump up their wings. Don't help. Wait for them to dry. Then let them go.

ask.q: What surprised you most in your butterfly's life?
good: How fast the caterpillar grew.
They looked like a bird dropping.
The chrysalis didn't move at all.
The wings were crumpled at first.

flow.do: Make a line chart of the caterpillar's length from the diary. Then finish with three sentences: what I think, what I saw and why.
flow.say: Let's turn your diary into a picture. Then tell me what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.kid: Draw a line chart from your diary. Then say: what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a caterpillar grows fast and then rebuilds into a butterfly. What I saw: they grew from 4 to 40 millimetres in about two weeks, moulted, then hung still for 10 days, and a butterfly came out. Why: the caterpillar stores up material by eating, and the chrysalis uses it to build the butterfly.

challenges.title: The Egg Lift: protect a raw egg
challenges.problem: A hen's eggshell protects the chick, but it can crack. Design a carrier that keeps a raw egg safe when it is dropped from 1 metre onto the floor.
constraints: Use only things from home, like paper, cloth, cotton, straws, rubber bands and boxes.
The carrier must fit inside a shoe box.
You can test it with a boiled egg first, then once with a raw egg.
materials: a boiled egg and a raw egg
paper, newspaper, cloth, cotton wool, straws, rubber bands, tape
a tray or old newspaper on the floor
general: Wrap the egg in something soft, like cotton or crumpled paper, so it slows down gently.
Hang the egg inside a box on rubber bands, so it bounces instead of hitting.
Make a paper parachute so the box falls more slowly.
creative: A hen's egg is strongest at its ends. Try standing the egg on its pointed end, held in a cup of folded paper.
Some seabirds that nest on cliff ledges lay long, pointed eggs. Try carriers of different shapes and see which lands best.
Build a tiny nest from twigs and grass, like a real bird would.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own carrier. Draw it, build it, test it with a boiled egg, and improve it. Then test once with a raw egg.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You build a carrier that keeps a raw egg safe when it is dropped from one metre, and learn how eggshells and nests protect chicks.

setup.art: A child wrapping a boiled egg in cotton wool inside a small cardboard box.
setup.caption: 1. Design and build a carrier for the egg.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a small box at the top of a measuring tape stuck to a wall, one metre up, over a tray.
setup.caption: 2. Drop it from 1 metre over a tray.

setup.art: A child opening the box and checking an egg for cracks with a magnifying glass.
setup.caption: 3. Open it and check for cracks. Improve and test again.

flow.do: 1. Gently press the two ends of a raw egg between your palms, over a bowl. 2. Then look at the shape of the egg.
flow.say: An eggshell is very thin, but its curved shape makes it strong. Press gently on the ends. It's hard to crack this way. Now, how could we keep it safe when it falls?
flow.kid: Hold an egg over a bowl. Press the two ends gently between your palms. Is it strong? Now design a carrier to keep it safe.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Egg Lift challenge. You feel how strong an egg's shape is, then design a carrier to protect it.

flow.do: 1. Draw a design. 2. Build it with a boiled egg inside. 3. Drop it from 1 metre over a tray. 4. Check the egg for cracks. 5. Improve it and try again.
flow.say: Draw it first. Then build it. Then test it. If it cracks, that's useful. It shows us what to change.
flow.kid: Draw your carrier. Build it. Drop it from 1 metre. Check for cracks. Make it better and try again.

check.q: In the Egg Lift, why does wrapping the egg in something soft help?
options: The soft stuff slows the egg down gently when it lands
The soft stuff makes the egg lighter
The soft stuff makes the shell thicker
check.why: When the box hits the floor, the soft wrapping squashes. That stops the egg slowly, not all at once, so the shell isn't hit so hard. Picking 'lighter' is a natural guess, but the egg weighs the same. What changes is how quickly it stops.

flow.do: Test the best design once with a raw egg. Then talk about how real eggs are kept safe.
flow.say: A real hen doesn't drop her eggs. She keeps them in a nest and sits on them. What does a nest do that your carrier also does?
flow.kid: Test your best carrier with a raw egg. Did it survive? How does a nest keep eggs safe?

ask.q: How do hens and other birds keep their eggs safe?
good: They make a soft nest.
They sit on them.
They hide the nest.
The shell is curved and strong.

challenges.title: Design a Butterfly Balcony
challenges.problem: Butterflies need two kinds of plants: plants with nectar for the adults to drink, and the right leaves for their caterpillars to eat. Design a balcony or window garden that gives a butterfly everything they need for their whole life cycle.
constraints: Use only space for 4 to 6 pots.
Every stage of the life cycle must be planned for: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and butterfly.
materials: a list of Indian butterfly plants from this challenge
optional: real pots, soil and seeds or small plants
general: Grow a curry leaf or lemon plant for lime butterfly caterpillars.
Grow flowers with nectar, like ixora, pentas or marigold, for the adults.
Leave some sticks and stems so caterpillars have a place to make a chrysalis.
creative: Put out a shallow dish of wet sand. Many butterflies sip salts from damp ground.
Plant a few kinds of host plants, so more kinds of butterflies can raise their young.
Keep a 'butterfly diary' of every visitor, and count them each week.

opts: All the stages of an animal's life, going round again
How many babies an animal has
quiz.why: A life cycle is the stages from egg or baby to adult. The adult makes new eggs or babies, so it goes round. Picking 'how many babies' is about one stage only.

quiz.p: Which is the right order for a frog?
quiz.why: Frogspawn hatches into tadpoles, which grow legs and become froglets, then frogs. The other orders mix up which stage makes which.

quiz.p: Which is the right order for a butterfly?
quiz.why: The caterpillar hatches from the egg and later makes the chrysalis. Picking 'egg, chrysalis, caterpillar' puts the chrysalis before the caterpillar. But the caterpillar is the one that makes it.

opts: A big change in body shape as a young animal grows up
Getting a bit taller each year
An animal moving to a new home
quiz.why: Metamorphosis is a big change of shape, like a tadpole becoming a frog. Picking 'getting taller' describes ordinary growing, like a chick or a child.

quiz.p: Which animal grows up WITHOUT metamorphosis?
quiz.why: A chick already looks like a small hen. They just grow. Frogs, butterflies and mosquitoes all change shape completely. Picking 'mosquito' usually means not knowing their babies are wrigglers in water.

quiz.p: What is the yolk of an egg for?
opts: Air for the chick to breathe
quiz.why: The yolk is the chick's food store. Air comes in through tiny holes in the shell, and there is an air pocket at the round end. Picking 'air' mixes up the yolk with the air pocket.
quiz.context: In Open an Egg like a Scientist, you cracked an egg and found all its parts.

quiz.p: How can a chick breathe inside their egg?
opts: Air comes through thousands of tiny holes in the shell
They hold their breath for 21 days
They don't need air until they hatch
quiz.why: The shell has thousands of tiny holes. You saw bubbles come out of them in hot water. Picking 'doesn't need air' is a common guess, but a growing chick needs oxygen all the time.
quiz.context: In the eggshell bubbles experiment, you put an egg in very hot water and saw tiny bubbles come out of the shell.

quiz.p: Where does a tadpole's tail go?
opts: It is broken down and used to build the frog
quiz.why: The tail cells break down on purpose. The blood carries the material to build legs, lungs and a new mouth. Picking 'falls off' is the most common guess. But nobody finds tails at the bottom of the pond.
quiz.context: Tadpole Watch is a monsoon experiment. You measure tadpoles' tails every second day as they turn into frogs.

opts: The caterpillar's body is broken down and rebuilt into a butterfly
The caterpillar sleeps and then wakes up with wings stuck on
quiz.why: Most of the caterpillar's body is broken down. Waiting cells grow into wings, legs and eyes, using that material. Picking 'nothing at all' is what it looks like from outside. Inside, it is the busiest stage.

quiz.p: Arjun, a boy in Class 3, writes down his caterpillar's length every day. Why is this useful?
opts: It shows a pattern he might not remember, like fast growth and then a stop
It makes the caterpillar grow faster
quiz.why: Writing measurements down lets you see patterns, like fast growth and then a stop before the chrysalis. Picking 'grow faster' or 'healthy' mixes up watching with changing. Measuring does not change the caterpillar.
quiz.context: In Raise a Lime Butterfly, you measured a caterpillar every day and kept a diary.

quiz.p: What switches on a tadpole's change into a frog?
opts: A hormone, a chemical message in their blood
quiz.why: The thyroid makes a hormone. When there is enough of it in the blood, the change starts. Picking 'eating flies' gets the order backwards. A tadpole eats insects only after they have become a frog.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still NOT know for sure?
opts: How much a butterfly remembers of being a caterpillar
That a chick hatches from an egg
quiz.why: Experiments with moths suggest some memory may survive, but scientists are still testing it. The other two have been watched and checked thousands of times.

quiz.p: A caterpillar ate leaves. The leaves were made from air, water and soil. Where did the butterfly's body come from?
opts: From the world around them, through the leaves
quiz.why: Every living body is built from material taken in from outside. It goes back to soil and air when the animal dies. Picking 'only from their egg' forgets that a caterpillar grows many times heavier by eating.

quiz.p: Meera, a girl in Class 3, cracks a shop egg onto a plate. She sees a yolk, the white and a tiny white spot. Where is the chick?
opts: There is no chick yet. In a fertilised egg kept warm, the spot would grow into one
Folded up small inside the yolk
Hidden inside the twisted white cords
quiz.why: A new egg holds no chick, only food, water and one tiny spot. In a fertilised egg kept warm, the spot grows into a chick, built from the yolk and white over 21 days. Picking 'folded up inside the yolk' is an old idea that scientists once held, until they watched eggs day by day.
quiz.context: In Open an Egg like a Scientist, you cracked an egg onto a plate and found all its parts.

applications: Poultry farms and hatcheries keep eggs in warm boxes called incubators for 21 days, turning them, to hatch chicks.
Health workers stop dengue and malaria by finding and removing still water where mosquito wrigglers grow.
Some towns put small fish that eat wrigglers into ponds and tanks, to break the mosquito life cycle.
India makes silk from the cocoons of silkworm moths: mulberry silk in Karnataka, tasar in Jharkhand, and muga and eri silk in Assam.
Farmers time their pest control to the right stage of an insect's life cycle, because caterpillars, not moths, eat the crops.
In many hospitals, doctors check a newborn baby's thyroid hormone, because this hormone helps babies grow.
Scientists use frogs and tadpoles to check whether ponds and rivers are clean, because their soft skin takes in what is in the water.
Butterfly parks and gardens grow both nectar plants and caterpillar food plants, so butterflies can finish their whole life cycle.
Fruit flies, which have a life cycle of about ten days, help scientists study genes and growth in laboratories.
Doctors study how a tadpole rebuilds their body to learn how wounds heal and how the body regrows parts.

open_questions.q: How did complete metamorphosis, with a pupa stage, first begin?
open_questions.why_open: It started more than 300 million years ago. Fossils of soft larvae and pupae are rare, so scientists rely on genes and living insects, and they still disagree.

open_questions.q: How much does a butterfly remember of being a caterpillar?
open_questions.why_open: A 2008 experiment with moths suggests some memory survives. But memory is hard to test in insects, and scientists don't know how it would pass through the rebuilding.

open_questions.q: How does each waiting cell inside a caterpillar know whether to become a wing, a leg or an eye?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know many of the genes involved. But how all the signals work together, at the right time and place, is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Why do some frogs skip the tadpole stage altogether?
open_questions.why_open: Some frogs in the Western Ghats hatch as froglets on land. Scientists have ideas, like avoiding fish in streams, but they can't yet say for certain which reasons mattered most.

open_questions.q: Why are frogs disappearing from so many places in the world?
open_questions.why_open: A skin disease caused by a fungus, loss of ponds, poisons and changing weather all play a part. How much each one matters is different in each place, and still argued about.

open_questions.q: What, if anything, does a pupa feel?
open_questions.why_open: We can't ask a pupa. Their nerves are being rebuilt. Nobody knows whether there is anything it is like to be a chrysalis.

open_questions.q: Could a body be taught to rebuild itself like a tadpole, to heal injuries in people?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists study tadpoles, which can regrow a lost tail at some stages. Using this in people is a hope, not yet a result.

maths.problem: In Tadpole Watch, a tadpole's tail was 18 millimetres long on day 20. On day 35 it was 8 millimetres long. How much shorter did it get?
maths.explain: The tail started at 18 millimetres and ended at 8 millimetres. To find the difference, take away: 18 minus 8 is 10. So the tail got 10 millimetres shorter. You can check by adding: 8 plus 10 is 18.
maths.context: In Tadpole Watch, you measure a tadpole's tail every second day, from outside the tub, as it turns into a frog.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting tells us exactly how much of the tail has gone into the body, instead of just saying 'it got smaller'.

maths.problem: A chick grows inside their egg for 21 days. How many weeks is that?
maths.explain: One week has 7 days. 21 divided by 7 is 3. You can check: 7 plus 7 plus 7 is 21. So a chick spends 3 weeks inside their egg.
maths.context: A hen sits on her eggs for 21 days before the chicks hatch.
maths.why_maths: Turning days into weeks helps you plan, for example to mark on a calendar when a chick should hatch.

maths.problem: Look at the caterpillar diary. On day 2 the caterpillar was 4 millimetres long. On day 16 they were 40 millimetres long. How many times longer were they on day 16?
maths.explain: On day 2 they were 4 millimetres. On day 16 they were 40 millimetres. 40 divided by 4 is 10. So they were 10 times longer. You can check: 4 times 10 is 40.
maths.context: In Raise a Lime Butterfly, you measure a caterpillar every day without touching it, and write their length in a diary.
maths.why_maths: Dividing tells us 'how many times bigger', which shows just how fast a caterpillar grows.

maths.problem: In the egg bubbles experiment, you counted trails of bubbles from the round half of the egg. Your tally was |||| |||| |||| ||. How many trails is that?
maths.explain: Each group of four lines with one line across makes 5. There are 3 full groups, so that is 3 times 5, which is 15. Then there are 2 more lines. 15 plus 2 is 17.
maths.context: In the eggshell bubbles experiment, you put an egg in very hot water and counted the thin trails of bubbles coming out of the shell.
maths.why_maths: Tally marks let you count quickly while you watch, without losing your place.

maths.problem: A lime butterfly spends about 4 days as an egg, 16 days as a caterpillar and 10 days as a chrysalis. How many days is that before the butterfly comes out?
maths.explain: Add the three stages. 4 plus 16 is 20. 20 plus 10 is 30. So it is about 30 days, about one month, from egg to butterfly.
maths.context: In Raise a Lime Butterfly, you watch a lime butterfly go through their stages: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and butterfly.
maths.why_maths: Adding the stages tells you how long the whole project will take, so you know when to expect the butterfly.

maths.problem: In the egg bubbles experiment, Lakshmi counted 17 trails of bubbles from the round half of the egg and 6 from the pointed half. Which end let out more air, and how many more trails did it have?
maths.answer: The round end, with 11 more trails.
maths.explain: 17 is more than 6, so the round end let out more air. 17 minus 6 is 11. This fits the egg: the air pocket is at the round end.
maths.context: In the eggshell bubbles experiment, you put an egg in very hot water and counted the trails of bubbles from each end.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two counts tells you which end lets out more air, and that points to where the air pocket is.

roots.context: We have been learning how a chick grows inside an egg and how a tadpole becomes a frog. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: The egg you opened held a yolk, a white and a tiny white spot, but no chick. If the egg is fertilised and kept warm, a chick takes shape in that spot. Their heart beats on day 2, their eyes form next, and their feathers grow from about day 9. A chick is built part by part over 21 days, from an egg that held none of those parts.
deep_truth.habit: We picture a tiny chick curled up in every egg, only waiting to grow bigger and hatch. Many scientists believed this too, in the 1600s and 1700s. In fact the egg holds the chick's food and a tiny spot, and the chick's parts are made one after another.
deep_truth.evidence: In Open an Egg like a Scientist, you found a yolk, a white, two twisted cords and a tiny white spot, but no chick. Scientists who open eggs on each day of warming see the heart, the eyes and the feathers form one after another. The chick video in this unit shows it too.

three.who_am_i: You also began as one tiny cell. Your body was built from the food your mother ate, and since then from your own food.
three.what_is_life: A living thing builds their new body out of food: a chick from their yolk, a frog partly from their tail, a butterfly from the caterpillar they were.
three.what_is_this_world: The yolk came from what the hen ate: grain, greens and insects. So every chick is built from the world around their mother.

roots.thread: A chick, a frog and a butterfly each build a new body out of material that is already there. The chick uses the yolk and white. The tadpole uses their own tail. The butterfly is built from the broken-down caterpillar. All of that material came from food, which came from plants, which were built from air, water and sunlight. So the same material passes from body to body, and takes a new shape each time.

teachings.source: Zhuangzi, chapter 2 (Discussion on Making All Things Equal), the butterfly dream
teachings.teaching: Zhuangzi, a Chinese thinker, dreamed he was a butterfly, happily fluttering. He woke up and was Zhuangzi again. Then he wondered: was he a man who had dreamed he was a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming he was a man? He said this is called 'the changing of things'.
teachings.link: A caterpillar becomes a butterfly and is still one living thing. Zhuangzi asks whether 'me' is as fixed as it feels.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to break open a tiny banyan seed. 'What do you see?' 'Nothing, sir.' Uddalaka says that from this fine, unseen thing the whole great banyan tree grows. 'That is the truth. You are that.'
teachings.link: Shvetaketu could see nothing inside the seed, yet a whole tree grows from them. The egg's tiny spot is the same: no chick is there to see, yet a chick grows from it.

teachings.source: Heraclitus, quoted by Plato in Cratylus 402a
teachings.teaching: Heraclitus, a Greek thinker, said that everything flows. You cannot step into the same river twice, because new water is always flowing in.
teachings.link: A body is like a river. Its material keeps changing, but the animal goes on. A tadpole's tail becomes part of the frog, and the frog goes on.

science.text: A growing chick takes calcium from the inside of their shell to build their bones. The shell gets thinner, which makes hatching easier.
Your own body rebuilds itself all the time. Your red blood cells last about four months and are then replaced.

other_view.who: Many biologists, and the Charvaka thinkers of ancient India
other_view.view: Many biologists say a growing chick or a changing tadpole is chemistry following genes, step by step. They say nothing more is needed to explain it. The Charvaka thinkers said only matter is real. Many careful people hold this view.

practice.title: Breathing in the egg
practice.say: Let's curl up small on the floor, like a chick inside an egg. Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly, and out slowly, five times. Be very still. A chick in their egg breathes too, through thousands of tiny holes in their shell. Feel the air going in through your nose. That air came from the room around you. Now, very slowly, uncurl. Stretch your arms out wide, as if you are breaking out of the shell.
practice.kid: Curl up small like a chick in an egg. Close your eyes. Breathe slowly five times. Feel the air come in. Now uncurl slowly. Stretch out wide.

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1600s and 1700s, many scientists believed that every egg held a tiny, ready-made chick. They thought the chick only had to swell up and hatch. This idea was called preformation. In 1759, a young German doctor, Caspar Friedrich Wolff, tested it. He opened hen's eggs after different numbers of days of warming, and looked at the growing chick under a microscope. He did not find a tiny chick that just got bigger. He saw blood vessels appear where there had been none, and new parts take shape step by step. In later work he showed that the chick's gut forms when a flat sheet of cells folds into a tube. So, Wolff said, the chick is built part by part out of material that has no shape at first. Famous scientists of his time, such as Albrecht von Haller, disagreed with him. But others who watched eggs day by day saw the same thing. In 1817, Christian Pander showed that the early chick is made of three thin layers, and each layer builds different parts. Today scientists agree that Wolff was right.
